items.body:
Chopstix, the UK’s leading Asian-inspired QSR brand, is launching two new stores in what is set to be a bumper week for the business, and its third store opening in August, bringing its bold, Chinese flavours to both Swindon and Gateshead.
Opening today in Swindon Designer Outlet, the new store is the second for the Southwest town and will create 20 jobs for locals and 20 covers to accommodate seated customers as well as takeaway and delivery. The store will boast the brand’s latest store design, featuring striking new visuals and updated in-store offerings such as self-order kiosks.
This marks the second opening in seven days for Chopstix, with the Swindon launch following the brand opening its doors in Newcastle’s Trinity Square, last Thursday. Opening in destination shopping locations such as Swindon and Gateshead is reflective of Chopstix’s wider growth strategy, expanding its store footprint in high footfalls areas that the brand has seen continued success with.
Gareth Brannigan, Head of New Store Openings, said: “These openings demonstrate the pace and ambition of our growth strategy as we continue to invest in locations where we know customers are looking for high-quality, great-value dining options.”
“Following the support of QSRP and the strong performance of our existing estate, we’re delighted to be opening in both Gateshead and Swindon, creating new jobs and bringing the latest Chopstix experience to even more communities. We look forward to welcoming customers through the doors in the coming weeks.”
A continuation of the surge of openings the brand has seen in 2026, these store openings follow investment from European quick service restaurant operator, QSRP, in October 2024. This expansion across the country is reflective of Chopstix’s wider growth strategy, growing its store footprint in high footfalls areas that the brand has seen continued success with.
With over 170 stores, the Chopstix Group has seen rapid growth over the past 12 months, in the UK and now France, having launched its second site on the continent earlier this week.
Chopstix was established in Camden Market in 2002 by entrepreneurs Sam Elia and Menashe Sadik, who remain involved with the business on a day-to-day basis. The Chopstix Group has undergone a busy period of brand development and expansion as Chopstix sets its sights on becoming the largest Asian QSR company on the continent.
For more information please visit: www.chopstixnoodles.co.uk

items.body:
With more than half of high-risk suppliers serving the UK retail sector lacking formal worker grievance channels, Antoine Heuty, senior vice president for Human Rights at EcoVadis, explains why retailers must close the gap between human rights commitments and conditions on the ground.
Retailers cannot address labour abuse they cannot see, and they cannot gain a reliable picture of conditions within their supply chains if workers have no safe way to speak.
When employees are unable to report unpaid wages, excessive overtime, harassment or coercion, serious human rights violations can remain hidden until they cause lasting harm to workers and significant legal, operational and reputational damage to businesses.
Retailers have invested heavily in human rights policies, supplier codes of conduct and social audits. These are important foundations, but they cannot alone reveal what is happening within factories, farms and other workplaces deep within global supply chains.
An EcoVadis report highlights the scale of this gap. It assessed 2,899 suppliers to UK retail and consumer goods companies between 2023 and 2025, including 242 based in countries classified as presenting a high risk of labour and human rights abuses.
Although 72% of these high-risk suppliers had a written human rights policy, 56% provided no formal channel through which workers could safely report labour-related concerns. Only 61% had introduced operational measures such as worker training, whistleblowing systems or third-party audits. Just one in five had reached an advanced level of maturity, combining a formal policy with at least four practical worker protection measures.
At the same time, the proportion of procurement by UK retail and consumer goods businesses coming from high-risk countries increased by 22% over two years. Retailers’ exposure is therefore rising precisely where the systems needed to identify and address exploitation remain weakest.
From policy to practice
A human rights policy is the beginning of due diligence, not its conclusion.
A commitment approved at corporate level has limited impact when a worker does not know it exists, cannot access a reporting channel in their own language or fears dismissal or retaliation if they raise a concern.
Traditional social audits only provide a partial picture. They are just a snapshot in time, and workers may be reluctant to speak openly when they do not trust that their identity will be protected.
Effective grievance mechanisms provide a more continuous source of intelligence. They help businesses identify emerging problems before they develop into systemic exploitation, supply disruption, public controversy or situations that are costly to manage.
However, establishing a telephone line or online form is not enough. A grievance mechanism is only effective when workers know about it, can access it easily, trust it and see evidence that concerns lead to action.
UK regulation is moving towards greater accountability
These findings come amid growing policy scrutiny of labour exploitation and forced labour in supply chains.
The recently introduced Immigration and Asylum Bill strengthens transparency expectations around forced labour, while the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner has called for more robust government action to prevent exploitation and hold organisations to account.
The Bill gives further impetus for businesses and organisations to take action as the Asylum Bill proposes changes to the reporting regime under section 54 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015. These cover: the requirement for an accuracy statement from the relevant signatory; extended scope to public bodies above a budget threshold; and financial penalties for non-compliance – up to £1 million or 1% of total turnover, whichever is greater.
For retailers, the direction of travel is clear. Publishing a modern slavery statement or supplier code will increasingly be viewed as insufficient. Businesses will need to demonstrate how risks are identified, what safeguards are operating within their supply chains and whether those measures are producing meaningful outcomes for workers.
Three priority actions for retailers
- Move to performance – prioritise supplier action rates over statement compliance in procurement due diligence.
- Close the consistency gap – apply heightened scrutiny to high-risk geographies, not just high-risk product categories.
- Centre the worker – require evidence that shows workers can access, understand and use grievance mechanisms in their own language, and that what they raise leads to a response. A modern slavery framework that doesn’t centre the worker is incomplete by design.
It should be noted that a higher number of complaints is not necessarily evidence that conditions are worsening. It may show that workers trust the system enough to use it. The critical measure is whether concerns are investigated and resolved.
Worker grievance mechanisms should not be treated as peripheral ESG initiatives. They are essential business controls that help retailers identify risks conventional monitoring can miss.
The findings expose a dangerous mismatch: sourcing from high-risk markets is increasing, while many workers most vulnerable to exploitation still lack a safe route to report it. Closing that gap is fundamental to protecting workers, meeting growing regulatory expectations and ensuring retailers can substantiate the human rights commitments they make.

items.title: Mike Ashley slams Burnham’s ‘populist’ plans to revive high street
items.summary: Retail tycoon Mike Ashley has blasted Andy Burnham’s proposals to revive the British high street as “populist” and “too little too late”. The billionaire Sports Direct and Frasers Group founder has written to the Prime Minister accusing him of failing to tackle the cost of living with “delusional” policies.  The causes of the UK’s rising [...]
items.body:
Mike Ashley slams Burnham’s ‘populist’ plans to revive high street
Retail tycoon Mike Ashley has blasted Andy Burnham’s proposals to revive the British high street as “populist” and “too little too late”.
The billionaire Sports Direct and Frasers Group founder has written to the Prime Minister accusing him of failing to tackle the cost of living with “delusional” policies.
The causes of the UK’s rising cost of living “have not been assisted by recent government policies and are not going to be helped by your recent populist proposals,” he said, in a letter seen by City AM.
Ashley accused Burnham of prioritising media attention over practical solutions to help households and business, taking aim at the Prime Minister’s “disastrous” position on business rates.
Burnham has pledged to review how business rates bills for pubs and hotels are calculated, and has previously supported a tax on warehouses to pay for lower taxes for high street shops.
Retailers have previously warned that a warehouse tax could push up prices for shoppers, and Ashley told Burnham that this tax measure would be “delusional”.
“Rather than address the real underlying issues of how the country’s financial affairs are managed, and supporting growth and entrepreneurialism in business, it is easier for you to pick topics which provide good media soundbites and the old salve of yet more regulation – which is not what the country needs to become competitive,” he wrote.
“Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer. You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong.”
Burnham resorting to ‘band wagons’
The retail billionaire mocked Burnham’s pledge to deliver “everyday fixes” on the cost of living, which have included a £2 bus fare cap and the removal of VAT on household electricity bills.
“This is a certainly a time for pragmatism and brave solutions but applying that to the underlying issues – not jumping on “everyday fixes” or band wagons that only address part of the problem,” he wrote.
Ashley’s intervention comes amid a growing backlash from business against Burnham’s pledges to tackle cost of living as costs facing businesses continue to rise.
On Monday, a group of influential business veterans including billionaire political donor John Caudwell and retail bigwig Lord Stuart Rose hit out at the “creep of taxes” hitting firms across the country.
In an open letter, the City grandees called on the government to rule out new taxes on founders, including levies on dividends, capital gains and business assets.
On Wednesday, Burnham told the Financial Times that he will tackle the “challenging” cost of business as he attempts to quash fears that October’s Budget will bring another damaging tax raid on British firms.
In the letter to Burnham, Ashley also hit out at the Prime Minister’s pledge to crack down on what he calls “fake” discounts. Aldi boss Giles Hurley has backed this initiative, accusing his supermarket rivals of misleading shoppers with loyalty pricing.
Ashley said: “The driving down of prices through discounting is what helps the consumer by giving them better value and helps with their cost of living. Driving down prices through discounting against an RRP can’t be what you really mean when you talk about “rip off Britain”.”
Before pushing into luxury fashion with Frasers Group’s acquisition of Harvey Nichols and stake-building in Hugo Boss, Ashley made his name by selling cheap sportswear at Sports Direct.

items.title: Bots and bargains: Zara owner launches cut-price Lefties in UK to rival Primark
items.summary: First robot-assisted outlet opens in Liverpool to take on Shein and supermarkets in clothing, shoes and homewares Business live – latest updates The owner of Zara is taking on Primark, Shein and the supermarkets with the launch of its cut-price chain Lefties in Britain, backed by an army of robots. The Spanish fashion brand opened its first UK store in Liverpool on Thursday, a few weeks after quietly launching its UK website. Continue reading...
items.body:
The owner of Zara is taking on Primark, Shein and the supermarkets with the launch of its cut-price chain Lefties in Britain, backed by an army of robots.
The Spanish fashion brand opened its first UK store in Liverpool on Thursday, a few weeks after quietly launching its UK website.
The store has embraced robotics to reduce staffing costs, with self-checkouts that scan a whole basket in one go and a clothes hanger sorter. Shoppers put their hangers in a slot as they pay and they are taken on a hidden conveyor belt to two robots behind a screen that sort them into boxes for different sizes.
The outlet at the Liverpool One city centre development also has fitting rooms equipped with a hatch through which unwanted items go to be sorted behind the scenes, again by robots.
The garment-sorting system splits clothes into rails for each department ready to be taken away to the shop floor or packed into the stockroom.
The Liverpool store is the first of three Lefties planned in the UK this year. The other two will be in the Lakeside shopping centre in Essex and the Metrocentre near Newcastle. More are expected next year.
Just before the official opening, as more than 100 customers queued up to be the first British shoppers, the chain’s general director said the group was “not thinking about a specific number” of UK stores and would look at how the first few went before taking next steps.
Xavier Ruz Riera said Liverpool had been chosen as the first outlet as it was a city with a vibrant young population that as a port was “open to the world” and “has a great personality”.
The Lefties name comes from the fact its owner, Inditex, launched it in 1999 as an outlet for unsold, or leftover, items from Zara. However, it stopped selling its bigger sister brand’s clothing about a decade ago, instead stocking its own range of men’s, women’s and children’s clothing, shoes, and homewares from bedding to vases.
As Zara has moved slightly upmarket, Lefties has stepped in as a more cost-conscious option. Its products are a touch above Primark but below Shein on price, with dresses an average of £18, compared with £16 at the British chain and £18.50 at the Chinese-founded marketplace, according to analysis by the trade journal Retail Week.
In a nod to the UK’s winter weather, the Liverpool store is the first Lefties to stock thermal clothing, presenting a new competitor to Marks & Spencer and Uniqlo on basic underwear, with bras from £7.99.
Riera said the store would flex to meet local demands, taking feedback from its sales figures and shop staff.
Its clothing and stores have more focus on design than Primark and it offers a nationwide online delivery service, unlike its British rival which only offers click and collect from its website. However, Lefties does not offer frequent discounts in the same way as Shein or other rivals such as Tesco’s F&F or Matalan.
Its garment-sorting machine is also in use at five UK Zaras, but the clothes hanger sorting system is a first for the group in Britain.
The chain operates in 20 countries including Italy, Turkey and Romania, with 225 stores globally. The brand, now Inditex’s fastest-expanding chain, opened its first French and Italian stores last year and is set to go into Germany in the spring.
Riera said: “The UK is a natural next step offering an exciting destination for our brand. We believe there is a strong opportunity to bring our proposition to UK customers, offering quality fashion and home collections for the whole family at accessible prices through a seamless in-store and online shopping experience.”
Lefties’ online store offers its full collection, with free delivery on orders over £49 and the ability to order or return items for free in store.
It is likely to add to pressure on cheaper clothing chains such as Primark, New Look and Matalan as well as online specialists including Asos, Shein and Boohoo. However, it faces a market crowded with competitors, including successful supermarket own labels such as Tesco’s F&F, George at Asda and Sainsbury’s Tu.
Lefties’ parent group’s decision to prioritise other markets over the UK is likely to reflect apprehension about the level of competition itcould face here.
Richard Lim, the chief executive of the industry analyst Retail Economics, said: “Lefties’ arrival in the UK reflects successive waves of disruption across the apparel market. Competition has intensified from Chinese commerce players such as Shein, while the huge momentum behind pre-loved platforms such as Vinted has further fragmented consumer spending.”
He added: “This is a direct challenge to Primark’s heartland. Lefties gives Inditex a stronger foothold in value fashion as the fight for the value-conscious fashion shopper is only getting more intense.”

items.body:
M&S is the first retailer to use AI-powered monitoring systems on its entire Milk Pool to monitor animal welfare across 46 dairy farms. The innovative tools use cameras to capture footage of dairy cows when they are indoors which is then analysed using an algorithm trained alongside vets to monitor welfare of dairy cows in real time. This latest move by M&S sets a new standard for animal welfare for dairy cows.
The technology uses AI-powered video analytics to build an individual health profile for each animal, tracking mobility and body condition scoring over time to give farmers objective, consistent data on the wellbeing of their herd. The tools monitor the cow’s behaviour including lying time, feeding time, social interactions and mobility to generate a ‘cow comfort score’ which supports vets in their assessment of individual cow’s health.
Regular, in person, welfare checks by independent vets will be enhanced by this daily monitoring of dairy cows. The cameras will assess body condition scoring to assess cows’ nutritional status over time. Terry Canning, CEO of Cattle Eye says “Changes in body condition are early indicators of metabolic health, fertility, and overall wellbeing. Tracking those changes more regularly, across every cow, gives farmers a level of insight that was previously unavailable outside research environments.” The algorithm supporting the tool has been tested and found to perform to the same standard as a trained welfare assessor.
These tools are being rolled out following trials at a selection of M&S dairy farms, where farmers have used the technology to make changes to tailor care to individual cow’s needs. By measuring lying times, farmers have made changes to the bedding of individual cows to improve their comfort based on their specific size and shape. Feeding schedules have been adapted to reduce the amount of time cows spend standing and the design of some stalls has been adapted to improve cow comfort.
Peter Kennedy, head of agriculture at M&S Food, said: “M&S has always had market-leading welfare standards, and as we continue to support British farmers in this latest evolution of welfare monitoring, powered by AI, it will support farmers to give the best care to dairy cows. This latest innovation supports our Plan A for Farming to build resilience in British farming and continue to raise the bar on animal welfare.”
Jenny Allan, Map of Ag Veterinary consultant, said: “M&S has had a longstanding focus on animal health and welfare, which has been in place for more than 15 years. Going forwards AI technology will enable real-time cow comfort and health parameters to be monitored, providing valuable insights across 46 farms.”
Terry Canning, CEO of CattleEye continues: “M&S has set a standard that the rest of the industry will be measured against. Deploying AI welfare monitoring across an entire supply chain is a first. This means we can give farmers and consumers peace of mind that productive herds can be healthy herds.”
M&S has invested more than £7m over the last decade in supporting farmers with agricultural innovation and a further £7m is available over the next five years. This is the latest innovation supported by M&S as part of its Plan A for Farming. Earlier innovations include a trial of flooring in the M&S-funded upgraded milking parlour, on one of the M&S Milk Pool farms, a trial measuring methane from Aberdeen Angus cows to support breeding a lower emission cow and last year a trial using the latest technology to farm a field of parsnips, delivering more, higher quality veg with a reduced carbon footprint.
M&S milk is 100% British and is sourced direct from 46 dairy farmers in its Select Farm milk pool. These close partnerships are the cornerstone of the most responsibly sourced milk on the market, ensuring animals and the environment are looked after and people on farms are set up for the future.

items.body:
Cheez-It is putting more weight behind the convenience channel with the launch of a 65g £1 price-marked-pack (PMP), giving wholesalers and independent retailers two proven flavour profiles in a format designed to drive impulse sales at a more competitive £1 price point.
Available now, the range brings together Cheese & Smokey Bacon and Double Cheese, giving retailers two distinctive flavours to drive interest to the singles fixture. Double Cheese is Cheez-It’s biggest-selling singles flavour, while Cheese & Smokey Bacon taps into growing consumer demand for bacon-flavoured crisps, snacks and nuts. Combining the bold taste of 100% real cheese with a rich, smokey bacon kick, every baked Cheez-It delivers the brand’s signature crunchy bite. Made with no artificial colours or flavours, the packs are ideal for on-the-go snacking.
Tapping into a format that accounts for almost seven in 10 convenience crisps sales, the launch comes as PMPs continue to play a significant role in the convenience fixture. PMPs now account for 80% of singles value sales across independents and symbols, with singles PMP value sales up 93% year on year.
For retailers, the £1 duo provides a straightforward way to build their singles fixture with two differentiated flavours at an accessible price point, while giving wholesalers an offer tailored to a format already established among their independent retail customers.
Rui Frias, senior marketing manager at Cheez-It, said: “Cheez-It has made a strong start in convenience with 1 in 2 shoppers coming back for more[4], and we’re continuing to build on that momentum by giving retailers the formats, flavours and price points that shoppers are looking for.
“The £1 PMP duo brings together the strength of our bestselling Double Cheese flavour with the growing appeal of Cheese & Smokey Bacon, creating an exciting proposition for the singles fixture. It’s another step in making Cheez-It an even stronger choice for retailers looking to drive impulse sales and give shoppers more reasons to pick up a pack.”

items.body:
Bio-Synergy is set to launch its Active Woman supplement range into Waitrose in August.
The launch will see the product range – including Activate protein, Energise creatine and Revitalise electrolyte mix, listed in 100 stores and at Waitrose.com, as part of the supermarket’s BrandsNew acceleration programme showcasing the most innovative and exciting challenger brands.
The Waitrose launch follows a redesign and relaunch for the Active Woman range, reflecting updated demand for supplements formulated for women that cater to the needs of an active lifestyle.
It also arrives as increasing numbers of women look for practical nutritional support while using or transitioning away from GLP-1 weight- management medication, when reduced appetite can make maintaining adequate protein, nutrient and fluid intake more challenging.
Activate provides a convenient source of protein, which contributes to the maintenance of muscle mass. Energise combines 4g of creatine monohydrate with 2g of hydrolysed marine collagen peptides, while Revitalise provides a refreshing electrolyte and vitamin drink for active days. Define combines glucomannan, green tea, chromium and caffeine in a convenient capsule designed to complement an active, balanced lifestyle. Together, the products provide a simple way for women to support their nutrition, strength, hydration and lifestyle goals without complicated routines or unnecessary noise.
The launch represents the latest major retail partnership for Bio-Synergy, whose products are also available through retailers including Selfridges, Superdrug, Holland & Barrett and Sports Direct.
Daniel Herman, founder and CEO of Bio-Synergy, said: “As a regular Waitrose customer, I have always felt it was the perfect home for the Active Woman range. I’m delighted that the Waitrose team shared my vision and recognised the opportunity to bring effective, straightforward nutrition to more women.
As a certified B Corp, we believe wellbeing should extend beyond the products we sell. That’s why every Active Woman customer can also claim a complimentary Active Woman Lifting Club session at gyms nationwide helping more women feel confident, get stronger and make it happen.”
Bio-Synergy’s Active Woman range will be available to shop at 100 Waitrose stores nationwide and online at Waitrose.com, from mid August, with prices from £17- £20.

items.title: Asda turnaround king Allan Leighton hopes for summer boost

items.body:
Asda turnaround king Allan Leighton hopes for summer boost
Allan Leighton, the turnaround expert charged with leading Asda’s resurgence, has been known for his showmanship. During his first stint at Asda in the 90s, he kicked off an annual managers’ conference by revving into the auditorium on a Harley-Davidson motorbike.
It was this reputation for bold, eye-catching leadership which prompted struggling discount retailer Asda to call on Leighton to halt its market share landslide. Leighton, now aged 73, may have put his Harley Davidson and leather cladding behind him, but the boardroom veteran is hoping to deliver some convincing evidence of progress on Friday.
The grocer’s latest trading update comes only a few weeks after it posted a £989m pre-tax loss for the year to December 2025 and saw revenue edge down by 3.6 per cent to £25.9bn. Asda has been cutting jobs in multiple departments, most recently at its head office in Leeds, as it attempts to slash costs and halt its market share declines.
The grocer, which is owned by private equity firm TDR Capital, has been weighed down by a huge debt pile in recent years. Asda’s net debt fell from £4.1bn to £3.5bn over the past year, according to its most recent accounts, but this remains a significant burden on the business.
Leighton first joined Asda in 1992, when he was poached by its then-chief executive – and current Marks & Spencer chairman – Archie Norman to lead its marketing department. Leighton became chief executive four years later and orchestrated the grocer’s turnaround and eventual sale to US retail titan Walmart, for a jaw-dropping £6.9bn.
Aldi and Lidl bring fresh competition
In 2000, Leighton quit Asda to “go plural” – a phrase he coined for taking on part-time directorships at several companies rather than focusing his efforts on one firm. Leighton held roles at Royal Mail, Leeds United, Pandora and the Co-op before returning to lead another Asda turnaround in November 2024.
He returned to a grocer in a far different state to how he left it – and facing a much-changed market. Asda has been assailed in recent decades by the meteoric rise of German discounters Aldi and Lidl, who mounted a serious challenge to the green-liveried grocer’s monopoly on low prices.
“It was a very one-dimensional market back then. Before we had online shopping, before we had smartphones,” says Ged Futter, a former Asda buyer who now trains suppliers to negotiate with supermarkets. “It was very much about the monthly shop, so it was a very different way of shopping.
“Back then, Asda was the price leader for retailers. Aldi and Lidl didn’t really exist, in terms of having any kind of impact at all.”
But Leighton is fighting to restore Asda’s reputation for low prices at a time when the German rivals have set a new standard for discounting. Even Tesco and Sainsbury’s, whose market shares appear unassailable, have been piling more products onto their Aldi price-match ranges.
“15 years ago, Asda took their eye off the ball when it came down to price, and they focused on the business, focused on profit, and that then allowed Aldi to own price,” Futter adds.
“There’s a reason why Tesco started off with Aldi price-match, because they know that Aldi own price. That’s what happened 15 years ago, and nothing’s changed.”
Leighton hails signs of turnaround
But Asda says Leighton’s turnaround is beginning to bear fruit. A spokesperson for the supermarket pointed to recent Worldpanel data which puts its market share at an unchanged 11.5 per cent, while sales dipped by 0.2 per cent in the year to August.
“This is Asda’s strongest performance since March 2024 and provides further evidence that the business is moving in the right direction,” they said.
At the grocer’s last trading update in March, Leighton said his plans are on track. “We have that momentum and a strong balance sheet to allow us to push forward.
“As we enter the second year of our turnaround, we have an improved customer offer, stable core systems, a strengthened balance sheet and a strong leadership team to deliver our formula for growth.”
Leighton said the group had notched 1.2 per cent sales growth in March, overturning months of declines, which he attributed to “progress in key areas” including pricing and availability.
The discount supermarket will hope to prove that this modest progress has been accelerated by a busy summer for British shoppers, during which multiple heatwaves and the FIFA World Cup have boosted other major retailers.
Competing for low prices is as difficult as it’s ever been. Morrisons, another private-equity owned grocer facing a hefty debt pile, announced earlier this week that it would match its five major competitors on the prices of 500 everyday products, including fish, bread and veg.
‘Leadership is everything’
Richard Hyman, an independent retail analyst, said: “I’m not suggesting that there are any forgiving sectors of retailing, but food is a really difficult market. Those players are all very, very good at what they do.”
Asda is hoping its buoyant non-food lines can lift its pursuit of rivals. Clothes retailing in particular is a bright spot for Asda, Hyman says. George, its own-brand fashion range, has been a “phenomenal success over the recent years,” he says.
The supermarket’s non-food revenue has accounted for about 14 per cent of its overall turnover in recent years.
Liz Evans, who has led George since 2022, announced her departure from the group in June. “Liz was outstanding to be able to deliver the numbers she did for George, given that their footfall is food-driven. […] Leadership is everything in all businesses, and especially in retailing,” Hyman said.

items.body:
How has your summer been? Done anything nice? As MPs prepare to head back to parliament next week, you’ll be relieved to hear that some of the most prominent figures in British politics have been enjoying the season’s cultural highlights – and without paying a penny. MPs throughout the Commons have received £400,000 of “freebies” to concerts, sports matches and other events so far this year, according to the most recent disclosures.
Over the summer alone, Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, enjoyed the Chelsea flower show thanks to Lloyds Banking Group covering the £1,839 cost, as did the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride. Lucy Powell, who has since become deputy leader of the Labour party and education secretary, accepted £858-worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group. Meanwhile, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, nabbed seats at Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.
Totalled up, MPs have been gifted £100,000 more so far this year than in the whole of 2025, with recipients seemingly learning few lessons from Keir Starmer’s “passes for glasses” scandal, in which a Labour peer gifted the then prime minister designer eyewear and clothes before being spotted in Downing Street with a temporary security pass.
Like many of these types of stories, there’s some nuance lurking behind the headlines. MPs quite rightly go to events linked to their constituency or local area. Andy Burnham accepting £3,800 tickets to the Brit awards in Manchester – when he was the regional mayor – to spotlight the city hosting the event for the first time is not the same as Streeting presumably just really wanting to meet Monty Don.
The increase can also partly be explained by the fact MPs have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on the parliamentary register after Starmer changed the rules, while ticket prices are well known to have gone up across the board. And yet, wade through the details of gigs and horse racing and it’s hard not to conclude some MPs are simply practising blatant grifting. Call it a treat for a seat, where our elected officials are enjoying must-see shows as a kind of unofficial bonus.
That much of this stuff was gifted by big business, including gambling firms and banks, makes the whole thing feel considerably grubbier. Why did the betting company Flutter want to shower then local backbencher and now chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, with high-priced tickets to the Grand National and Cheltenham?
Public perception of such luxury perks will be even more unforgiving against a backdrop of an ongoing cost of living crisis. A night at the Ivor Novello awards may not be the duck house-level opulence of 2009’s expenses scandal, but the optics are little better. While much of the population are struggling to pay their electric and food bills, MPs are getting out the fascinators for Ladies’ Day at Aintree.
Politicians, of course, are human. Who among us wouldn’t be tempted by Harry Styles? The electorate, for its part, tends to want leaders to connect with everyday life. There’s a reason why Malcolm Tucker in The Thick of It – based on the rumour Alastair Campbell got Tony Blair clips of EastEnders and reality shows – makes a “zeitgeist tape” to help his useless ministers seem “in touch”. But it would be disingenuous to pretend MPs are driven to accept hospitality gifts as a bid to be down to earth, or that balancing such demands from the public is somehow a complex, grey area. Most people like to see their MP letting loose at a concert – they just want them to have paid for their ticket.
With the standards watchdog due to question Nigel Farage when parliament reopens – an inquiry he temporarily dodged by calling a byelection – the coming weeks will very likely see a renewed focus on what MPs receive and the transparency around it.
On paper, Farage’s gifts are in another league to his colleagues’ freebies: forget a ticket to the tennis, we’re talking £5m from a crypto billionaire and further “financial support” from a convicted fraudster. And yet to a public who have for decades seen front-page stories about politicians’ finances – from expenses and second jobs to tax avoidance – the idea that the Reform UK leader is an outlier worth investigating rather than one of a bad bunch can feel at best a hard sell and, at worst, hypocritical.
If MPs wish to be able to hold Farage to account with credibility, they will need to show they care about cash and transparency in every form. That means the government looking harder into how some MPs are using their influence to make extra money, not least when it’s linked with the growth of the far right. Just this week it emerged that the Restore leader, Rupert Lowe, is set to earn as much from his – anti-migrant – posts on X as he does from his MP’s salary (which he gives to charity) since Elon Musk took over and financially rewarded some high-reach posts. “Gifts” come in many forms.
Winning public trust will also require MPs to be squeaky-clean themselves and stop accepting hospitality unless it’s linked to their constituency – even if that means watching the Chelsea flower show on iPlayer like the rest of us.
Because every time an MP goes to an event for free, it comes with a hidden cost: a public with ever-decreasing faith in the political class, who are more likely to greet outright corruption or cronyism with a weary shrug. “They’re all the same” is a dangerous public mood for a democracy and one that, once embedded, can be deeply hard to dislodge.
- 
  Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Developed and launched in a record time of just eight weeks, the new gift cards give DIY enthusiasts and trade professionals total flexibility to purchase and redeem gift cards across all Toolstation touchpoints. This includes in-store across its network of over 590 UK branches, online, or through the Toolstation mobile app. The programme enables new brand activation for Toolstation and serves as an opportunity to further build customer engagement, loyalty and revenue.
Powered by EPS’s API-based payments platform, the programme provides Toolstation with end-to-end card processing capabilities, including real-time top-ups, balance enquiries, and secure redemptions built directly into Toolstation’s checkout systems with zero third-party redirects. EPS also equips the Toolstation team with dedicated customer service management tools and advanced analytics dashboards to monitor activity, breakage, customer behaviour, and campaign performance.
From the initial conversation, EPS understood the opportunity for Toolstation to introduce a gift card offering and consulted with key stakeholders at Toolstation on industry and product best practices. After defining the product requirements, Toolstation set an ambitious launch target and recognised Edenred Payment Solutions as well placed to deliver on this.
Rehana Mitha, Managing Director at Edenred Payment Solutions, said, “Toolstation is the latest retailer to recognise the importance of incorporating gift cards into their customer proposition. They wanted to create a brand new programme with zero friction when their customers were using the gift card, regardless of how they choose to purchase and redeem across stores, the web and app. They set an ambitious goal of integration, card manufacture, and launch in their stores in just eight weeks. Our dedicated project team worked with great agility and close collaboration with several Toolstation stakeholders to meet this timeline. We are thrilled to support Toolstation with an end-to-end payment solution that promotes long-term customer loyalty while also giving rise to meaningful community and B2B initiatives in the future.”
Key benefits of the programme

- Complete channel choice: Buy and spend seamlessly across the web, app, or in-store.

- Frictionless experience: Smooth purchasing and redemption are integrated directly into existing user journeys.
For Toolstation:
- Incremental revenue: Acquire new customers, guarantee future spend, and boost average order values.
- Loyalty enhancement: Integrate with Toolstation’s existing loyalty initiatives, allowing gift cards to be used as promotional incentives and competition rewards.
“We know our customers value speed, convenience, and flexibility above all else, which is why we have introduced a gift card offering,” said Chris Other, Customer Director at Toolstation. “By making our cards redeemable across our app, website, and in-store, we’re making it easier than ever for tradespeople to get the products they need.

Finsbury Food Group is expanding its Little Big Cake range with the launch of a strawberry matcha flavoured cake arriving exclusively in Tesco stores nationwide from 31st August.
Inspired by matcha lattes which have been taking coffee shops and social media feeds by storm, this new cake has been developed with millennial and gen z consumers in mind. The cake, called I Like You Berry Matcha, transforms one of the biggest drinks trends to the supermarket aisle in a unique way.
Standing taller than a traditional celebration cake, the four-layer, five-inch diameter cake has a narrower profile inspired by the shape of a matcha take-away cup. It features alternating vanilla and pink sponge, and is layered with strawberry jam as well as matcha, white chocolate and strawberry frosting, finished with a dusting of matcha powder.
Each layer has been designed to bring something different, allowing the strawberry, matcha, vanilla and white chocolate flavour profiles to shine through individually before coming together in every slice.
Weighing 970g, serving up to 12 people and available with an RRP of £16, the cake is a ‘matcha’ made in heaven for birthdays, get-togethers and smaller celebration moments. Its eye-catching green, pink and white design makes it the perfect option for taking to a friend’s house or sharing on your social feed.
The launch from Finsbury Food Group aims to fill a gap for shoppers who may have outgrown traditional character cakes but still want something colourful, contemporary and worthy of a place on the grid. As matcha continues its evolution from a Japanese ritualistic ingredient to a mainstream trend, Finsbury is giving more shoppers the chance to discover it in an accessible and joyful format.
Kimberley Curtis, brand manager at Finsbury Food Group, said: “Finsbury’s own brand, Little Big Cake, gives us the freedom to look at what’s happening across food culture and turn those trends into something that’s never been done before”
Ross Lowrey-Heywood, innovation development manager at Finsbury Food Group, said: “Matcha is no longer a niche ingredient. It has become one of the biggest coffee shop trends of the moment, embraced for its flavour, colour, ritual and unmistakable aesthetic. Coffee shops have been leaning into cake for some time, so it felt only right that cake should lean into matcha.
“With this cake, we wanted the individual flavours and colours to stand out. It’s vibrant, playful and completely different from anything else in the supermarket cake aisle. We’ve taken the matcha trend and reimagined it as a celebration cake and we think shoppers are going to like it very matcha!”
The Little Big Cake brand was launched by speciality bakery manufacturer, Finsbury Food Group, in January 2026 when it brought the first cake bento box to market for UK supermarket shoppers.

Halfords lifts profit targets on heatwave boost
The sun has shone on Halfords’ summer trading as the motoring and cycling retailer lifted its profit targets in response to “very strong” recent sales.
The FTSE 250 firm had previously been tipped for a £52.6m pre-tax profit this year but said on Thursday that it now hopes to make between £55m and £65m. Shares in Halfords roared on Thursday morning, gaining 11 per cent to 269p.
In an unscheduled update to investors, the group said it has “outperformed” in recent months due to higher-than-expected sales in its summer ranges.
“This reflects momentum in the underlying business as we continue to deliver against our strategic priorities alongside a very strong performance in seasonal categories, in part reflecting unusually warm summer weather,” Halfords said on Thursday.
Higher demand for seasonal products alone has boosted the retailers profit by millions of pounds, it estimated.
The group is best-known for selling bikes and offering cycle and motoring repair services but also sells assorted seasonal goods like camping and barbecue gear.
Analysts at RBC Capital Markets said that the retailer’s cycling, camping and air conditioning ranges were likely behind this summer trading boost.
Halfords will invest some of this extra cash into its tech and marketing departments, it said, meaning that its full-year performance will be weighted towards the first half.
‘Early signs’ of turnaround progress
The retailer’s share price had been in steady decline since 2021, after it failed to replicate its huge boost in pandemic-era sales as bored Brits flocked to cycling.
Last April, former chief executive Graham Stapleton announced his sudden departure after seven years at the helm. He was replaced by former Very boss Henry Birch, who has led a rapid expansion of the group’s network of garages.
In June, shares in Halfords leapt 14 per cent after it smashed analyst expectations to turn a £44m pre-tax profit, reversing the previous year’s £30m loss.
“Halfords has a strong market position in the UK motoring and cycling markets, with a good offer in both the retail and services sectors. We are encouraged by a more resilient performance from the motoring and cycling markets,” analysts at RBC said.
“We are encouraged by the early signs of progress from Halfords’ ‘Fit for the Future’ plan, but we do note ongoing macroeconomic and political uncertainty which may weigh on the more discretionary areas of [Halfords’] offer,” they added.

The City’s largest hedge funds, insurers and pension funds are racing to prepare for sweeping rules that will stop nearly 40,000 companies from hiding bullying and harassment cases from the financial watchdog.
From the start of next month, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will expand a crackdown on bad behaviour in the banking industry to a wider group of City investment firms and brokers.
Under the rules, companies will be expected to report any serious cases of non-financial misconduct to the regulator. The firms will also be required to pass on reports of bad behaviour – including racism, sexual harassment, violence and intimidation – to a manager’s prospective future employer. It is hoped that the rules will prevent cases of “rolling bad apples”, where rogue bosses move to new firms without facing consequences.
The FCA’s expanding crackdown beyond financial crime has so far focused on the banking sector. However, with new rules looming for thousands of additional firms, experts say hedge funds, investment managers, insurers and brokers are racing to train their staff and to wrap up any internal investigations before the rules come into force.
“The countdown is now on for regulated firms to be ready for the new rules taking effect in September,” said Jill Lorimer, a partner at the law firm Kingsley Napley, who focuses on financial regulation. “We are aware of firms brushing up their policies and procedures in this area and ensuring training has been thoroughly refreshed and completed.
“Firms dealing with allegations against their people now may want to ensure that these processes are wrapped up before the new regime takes effect. The FCA will no doubt be looking for cases in this area to show it is willing to flex its muscles.
“The City should take these changes very seriously indeed, as no firm will want to be the target of high-profile regulatory attention,” she added.
The new rules will apply to any company bound by the FCA’s senior managers and certification regime, which holds top bosses accountable for wrongdoing.
It comes despite a regulatory pushback by City firms and some politicians who complain red tape in the finance industry is holding back investment, jobs and growth in Britain.
However, a recent spate of misconduct cases have strengthened the argument that cleaning up the financial sector could create a competitive advantage, particularly for an industry long-criticised for operating a boys’ club culture.
That includes the case at Lloyd’s of London, which recently revealed that its former boss John Neal failed to disclose a “close relationship” with a female colleague. The insurance market operator also said that whistleblower reports dating back to 2023 had been mishandled, in a breach of its own governance rules.
A recent court battle against the former Barclays chief executive Jes Staley also appears to have strengthened the FCA’s resolve. Last year, judges upheld a decision by the City watchdog to ban Staley from holding a senior finance industry role in future, after he was found to have misled the regulator over the nature of his relationship with the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The FCA is now hoping for similar success in a court battle with the hedge fund boss Crispin Odey. The Brexit-backing investor is trying to overturn a ban on him holding senior roles in the UK finance industry, after the FCA said he deliberately tried to frustrate an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment against him at his hedge fund.
Those allegations have been extensive, with a Financial Times investigation reporting allegations of sexual assault and harassment against Odey from 20 women.
Odey has denied those allegations. He also said in a witness statement that he had not tried to prevent an investigation, and had been treated unfairly by the FCA.
Commenting on the expansion of its non-financial misconduct rules, an FCA spokesperson said: “When bullying, harassment or violence goes unchallenged, it raises wider questions about a firm’s culture, and ultimately harms confidence in financial services.
“Our rules and guidance will help industry take a more consistent approach. But the primary responsibility for preventing and dealing with this behaviour remains with firms.”

items.body:
Britain’s high streets are facing a confidence challenge, but new research launched by retail and shopper marketing agency Savvy, suggests younger shoppers are significantly more optimistic about their future. Carried out among 1,005 UK shoppers, the findings indicate that 41% of shoppers overall feel positive about the future of UK high streets. Among Gen Z, however, that figure rises sharply to 64%.
The findings also point to strong public appetite for action – 85% of shoppers support greater government investment to improve UK high streets. The research comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham unveiled new measures aimed at reviving Britain’s “hollowed out” high streets, giving local communities and councils greater powers to shape their town centres.
Savvy’s findings suggest shoppers have not given up on the high street, however they are also clear about what could make them more appealing. More than a third (37%) strongly agree they would be more attractive if they featured more independent businesses, while 35% strongly agree that too many high streets look the same because they contain the same chain stores.
Catherine Shuttleworth, CEO of Savvy Marketing, commented: “It would be easy to assume that the most digitally connected generation would have the least interest in the high street, but our research suggests the opposite. Gen Z is considerably more positive about its future.
“For this generation, online and offline aren’t necessarily competing worlds. They might discover a brand on TikTok and still want to experience it physically, particularly when shopping is part of a wider day out or something they can do with friends. That creates a real opportunity for high streets to bring together digital discovery, physical experience and social connection.”
The research suggests shoppers increasingly want high streets to offer more than retail alone. Eight in ten respondents agreed that high streets should focus on leisure and experiences as well as shopping.
Their community role remains important too. Nearly a third (31%) strong agree that high streets should focus on leisure and experiences as well as shopping, with 49% tending to agree.
Together, the findings point towards a broader role for the high street: one that combines shopping with leisure, experiences, services and social connection. Rather than trying to recreate the high street of the past, the opportunity is to understand what will give people reasons to spend time there – whether that is independent retail, places to eat and drink, health and wellness, services or experiences – while recognising that the right mix will differ from one community to another.
Shuttleworth added: “There is clearly an appetite for high streets to evolve, but shopper enthusiasm alone won’t be enough. If we want independents, entrepreneurs and emerging brands to take space, high streets also need to be viable places in which to operate.
“Investment is important, but so is creating an environment where businesses can realistically make the numbers work. Get that right, alongside a more compelling mix of retail, experiences and community, and there is a real opportunity to give people new reasons to come back to the high street.”

items.title: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis
items.summary: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme . items.body:
Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme.
He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months.
Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting.
“It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.”
A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years.
But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated.
“I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people. The last thing we want to see is a diagnosis of problems leading to a life on benefits.”
At a roundtable discussion, McFadden asked each of the young people how they felt as a result of their move into paid work. They cited better social lives and clearer daily routines.
“I’m so conscious, having done this job for almost exactly a year now, that belief and confidence is a big part of the picture,” McFadden told journalists afterwards. “We mustn’t blame young people for the challenges they are facing in the labour market.”
The number of Neets in the UK recently topped 1 million – with the latest data due out on Thursday.
Alan Milburn, the Blair-era cabinet minister reviewing youth inactivity for the government, has warned that the number could hit 1.25m by 2030, without intervention. His final report is due in the autumn.
McFadden made clear that welfare reform would probably be part of the government’s response, criticising the “black and white” distinction in the current universal credit system.
“There’s a design flaw in the universal credit system, which too readily separates people into ‘fit for work’ and ‘unfit for work’, and when they are unfit for work, leaves them without any support or any conditions,” he said. “That’s what I call the culture of ‘signed off and written off’. I think we need to change that.”
He highlighted a recent initiative under which claimants with no obligation to look for work have been asked to attend voluntary interviews with work coaches at their local Jobcentre.
McFadden had started the day at a branch of Sainsbury’s in London, stacking shelves in the bread aisle, alongside the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan.
The trio were highlighting the fact that Sainsbury’s is offering 10,000 internships for young people.
McFadden praised Boots and Sainsbury’s, and encouraged other big employers to play their part in what he called the “national cause” of tackling youth unemployment.
Asked whether it was a good use of public money to be subsidising corporations to take on young people, he said: “I’m enthused when businesses like Boots or Sainsbury’s – or any business in the country – steps up and says: ‘I want to play my part here.’ And if there’s a bit of a financial incentive in it, that’s fine.”
The jobs guarantee scheme will eventually be available to 18- to 24-year-olds in Great Britain who have been claiming universal credit and seeking work for at least 18 months, with the aim of creating 90,000 subsidised placements over the next three years.
It is initially being piloted in six areas with high unemployment, including central and east Scotland, Birmingham and Solihull, and south-east and south-west Wales. The government intends it to be nationwide by November.

items.title: Plug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first time
items.summary: DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity Plug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity. Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers. Continue reading...
items.body:
Plug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity.
Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers.
Argos will be the first to offer the DIY solar systems this week, helping people living in flats or rented homes without roof access to lower their bills by generating their own electricity.
The rival retailers Amazon, Currys, B&Q and Screwfix are also expected to stock their shelves with plug-in panels within the coming weeks at prices starting from about £400 to £500 depending on the capacity of the system.
The devices are already popular in Spain and Germany, where they are known as Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant) because they can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.
The solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid. Each solar system must be registered so Great Britain’s National Energy System Operator can gauge how the cumulative impact of these panels could cut the need for gas-fired power or imports.
In the UK the 800-watt solar systems due to go on sale will be about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar set-up, meaning they are unable to provide enough energy to power a home but they could save the average household up to £110 a year on their annual electricity bill.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Plug-in solar is a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away.”
Graham Biggart, the managing director for Argos, said: “By making this technology more accessible, we’re putting more power in the hands of our customers and helping them explore practical ways to manage energy use at home.”
The savings possible from each solar system will depend on how much solar power is generated, which could be affected by the orientation of each solar panel and the weather on any given day.
Savings will also depend on whether the household is able to use the electricity while it is being generated – perhaps by running washing machines or dishwashers during sunny spells – because plug-in batteries were not included in the new legislation allowing plug-in solar sales to begin.
Emily Seymour, the energy editor at the Which? consumer group, said: “These smaller systems will generate less electricity than conventional rooftop solar and won’t be suitable for every home. People may need planning permission or the consent of the building owner before going ahead, so it will be important to check your own circumstances before making a purchase.
“There are also important safety considerations, particularly around the suitability of older electrical systems, the safe mounting of panels and the potential for people to use products or equipment incorrectly.”
Joanna O’Loan, a manager at Energy Saving Trust, said: “While the savings will vary from home to home, plug-in solar panels will give more people greater control over their energy use and costs. As these products become more widely available, access to clear and reliable information is essential to help people make informed choices that are right for their home and budget.”

The listing debuts Collider’s new four-pack format, created for grocery.
Harry Cooke, founder of Collider, said: “We built Collider on a simple idea: take the alcohol out of beer and put something better in. Most alcohol-free beer asks you to settle for less. items.body:
Blue Yonder, the AI company for supply chain, today announced new retail innovations as part of its Cognitive Solutions portfolio, designed to help hardlines and softlines retailers move from insight to action with agentic AI and connected retail decisioning. The latest enhancements create tighter alignment across forecasting, inventory planning, fulfilment, customer service and returns on the Blue Yonder Platform. Retailers can now respond faster to changing demand, improve inventory productivity and recover more value across the retail lifecycle. Rather than optimising individual retail functions in isolation, Blue Yonder connects decisions across planning and execution, so what a retailer learns about demand shapes both how they fulfil and how they manage returns.
“Many retailers can already see what’s happening. The hard part is acting on it before the moment passes,” said Gurdip Singh, chief product officer at Blue Yonder. “With this release, we’re putting agentic AI into the flow of retail decisions. Forecasting, inventory, fulfilment and returns start working as one system instead of a chain of handoffs. That’s how you turn insight into action at the speed retail demands, with the precision to protect margins while you improve the customer experience.”
What analysts are saying
“Fulfilment networks are getting more complex, and customers aren’t waiting for retailers to catch up,” said Ananda Chakravarty, VP Research, Retail, IDC. “Winning retailers are connecting inventory visibility, order management, returns, warehouse and transportation into one AI-driven decision engine, not five different engagement platforms. That’s the difference between fast, profitable fulfilment and margin bleed. There’s no more room for disconnected execution.”
Smarter fulfilment and inventory visibility
Poor availability is expensive. Out-of-stocks cost retailers roughly $1.2 trillion a year in lost sales, according to IHL Group. The release adds predictive fulfilment intelligence and inventory network visibility in Order Management. This helps teams improve fill rates, service levels and fulfilment efficiency by identifying risks, bottlenecks and optimisation opportunities across inventory, sourcing, fulfilment and network operations. For retailers, that means better availability, fewer missed promises and smarter fulfilment decisions across stores, distribution centres and digital channels.
Unified workspace for service and selling
A new unified customer service and assisted selling workspace streamlines customer identification, product discovery, inventory visibility, pricing, fulfilment options, payment capture and order management. Customer service and store teams can respond faster, improve conversion and resolve issues with better context.
Recovering more value from returns
Returns are among retail’s costliest problems. U.S. consumers were expected to return nearly $850 billion in merchandise in 2025, about 15.8% of sales, according to the National Retail Federation. Blue Yonderbrings new omni-inventory capabilities across online, warehouse and store returns. This new functionality includes:
- Personalised returns experiences
- Customer-specific returns policies
- Configurable store credit strategies
- Returns order receiving and receipt control
- Smart Disposition and configuration
- Test and Grade workflows
- Unit-level simulation of disposition outcomes
Together, these capabilities target the same problems: reduce returns 
“For most retailers, a return is a cost to absorb. I’d argue it’s a chance to reimagine the customer experience, save the sale and optimise inventory,” Singh said. “Now, the system doesn’t just initiate and process the return. It recommends the best decision for that item and allows users to act on it, from routing to receipt to resale. That’s an agent that does the work and helps recover more margin without adding headcount.”
AI-guided workflows with Orchestrator
Blue Yonder enhances Orchestrator as the unified interaction and orchestration layer for workflows, insights, AI-powered guidance and actions. A new navigation experience combines traditional navigation with a prompt-driven, AI-first experience, so people move from decision to action faster across planning, execution and network operations.
More updates across planning and forecasting
The release includes several other updates:
- Assortment Planning adds assortment strategy and scoring guidance, demand explainability, in-season sales and inventory planning, and placeholder store workflows.
- Allocation and Replenishment adds returns projections, enhanced multichannel forecasting and automated supply distribution when inventory arrives at the distribution centre.
- Space Planning Solution adds closed-loop planogram execution and compliance capabilities that connect planning to in-store implementation, validate execution against actual shelf conditions, and continuously improve planograms through feedback to planners.
Together, the updates give retailers one connected system to plan, decide and act on with speed and precision. The enhancements are available now as part of Blue Yonder Cognitive Solutions.

items.title: The London stock market dodged a bullet with Shein | Nils Pratley
items.summary: China’s fashion giant will list in Hong Kong with a shrunken price tag – and big questions over its business model In a parallel world, we might now be preparing for the arrival on the London stock market of Shein , the giant Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer. Or it could have happened already. The possibility of a London flotation was a running story during 2024 and into last year as politicians from both main parties engaged in behind-the-scenes wooing. Shein was seen as a shot of tech adrenalin for a listless local listings scene, and an opportunity to advertise the UK’s openness to international capital. Continue reading...
items.body:
In a parallel world, we might now be preparing for the arrival on the London stock market of Shein, the giant Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer. Or it could have happened already.
The possibility of a London flotation was a running story during 2024 and into last year as politicians from both main parties engaged in behind-the-scenes wooing. Shein was seen as a shot of tech adrenalin for a listless local listings scene, and an opportunity to advertise the UK’s openness to international capital.
Instead, Shein will float next week in Hong Kong. To which one can only say: thank goodness for that.
In a listings context, Shein was a cast-off. The company had rejected New York amid tensions between Washington and Beijing and hostile questions from US lawmakers over labour practices in its supply chains in China. London was merely the next-best option for a company whose owners seemed suspiciously anxious to find a stock market home in the west.
London did its reputation no favours with its willingness to jump. The Financial Conduct Authority, in charge of listings, took the view that it was “not unusual” for UK-listed companies to carry legal risks around the world and that what mattered was disclosure to allow investors to form their own view. The Labour government sounded keen. Donald Tang, the banker hired as Shein’s chair, did a round of feelgood meetings.
This positivity was punctured, however, in January last year when Shein’s general counsel in Europe appeared at the Commons business select committee and stone-walled.
Did Shein source cotton from China, asked the committee chair, Liam Byrne. The company representative was not qualified to reveal such “detailed operational information”. Byrne had not even been asking at that point about allegations of use of cotton produced in the Xinjiang region, which has been linked to Uyghur forced labour.
The company, it should be added, had already said it had signed statements of compliance to modern slavery acts in the US, UK and elsewhere. But Byrne’s view was entirely fair: “The reluctance to answer basic questions has frankly bordered on contempt of the committee.”
The idea of listing in London soon went away – encouraged, it seemed, by pressure from Beijing. And so, Hong Kong it is.
Note, though, how the company’s price tag has shrunk from the £50bn that was talked about during the London leg of the global tour. The valuation will be $27bn (£20bn).
That figure also reflects the other issue that has dogged Shein: political and societal resistance to the practice of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods. The US has already closed such “de minimis” exceptions as part of President Trump’s tariffs wars; the EU says it will phase them out; the UK intends to get there by 2029. Shein used to argue that its business model did not depend on tax breaks, but the reduced valuation suggests that investors do not regard the issue as irrelevant.
In a world in which Shein had somehow managed to list in London last year, the valuation drop would have been felt here. The supposedly hot prize would look substantially less so. London dodged a bullet on this one. Those politicians who encouraged the flirtation might reflect that, while the stock market is obviously desperate for exciting newcomers, you’ve got to choose your targets carefully. Nobody is talking about a missed opportunity.

items.title: Pubs, bars and hotels report ‘Burnham bounce’ in optimism but call for further tax relief
items.summary: Sentiment in hospitality and brewing sectors more positive since business rates action, trade bodies’ survey finds Pubs, bars and hotels have reported a “Burnham bounce” in optimism as a result of the prime minister’s overtures to the sector, polling suggests, but they warn that the goodwill could evaporate without further tax relief. items.body:
Pubs, bars and hotels have reported a “Burnham bounce” in optimism as a result of the prime minister’s overtures to the sector, polling suggests, but they warn that the goodwill could evaporate without further tax relief.
Andy Burnham has positioned himself as a staunch ally of the UK’s hospitality industry both before and since his arrival at No 10, last month announcing a discount on business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
The result, according to a survey by multiple trade bodies, is that 37% of businesses in the sector now feel that his government will benefit hospitality and brewing, which are collectively worth about £100bn to the economy.
The degree of optimism is more than double the 18% recorded before the policy on business rates was announced, an increase described by the trade bodies as a “Burnham bounce”.
The government has signalled further reform of business rates to ease pressure on the sector. But with the details still uncertain, some venue owners have warned that the steps taken so far have done very little to reduce their groaning pile of rising costs.
The survey findings, shared with the Guardian, also show that the industry believes the tax burden – in particular VAT – is continuing to hold back the sector.
Three-quarters of respondents pointed to tax as the biggest barrier for businesses, with political instability (37%) cited as the second biggest.
The survey was compiled by the British Beer & Pubs Association, UK Hospitality, the British Institute of Innkeeping, and Hospitality Ulster.
“The new prime minister’s action to back hospitality has clearly driven a boost in the sector’s optimism, yet significant challenges remain,” said the trade bodies in a joint statement.
“The support for pubs and live music venues on business rates was a great first step, and now we need to see wider support and conditions to allow the entire hospitality sector to grow and create jobs.
“Our tax burden – amongst the highest in the economy – along with new regulatory costs is overwhelming us and the real victims are high streets, jobs, and communities. A lower rate of VAT, wider permanent business rates reform and changes to employer NICs [national insurance contributions] would help deliver the prime minister’s bold ambitions for every postcode.”
More than 330,000 people have signed a petition calling on the government to cut VAT on hospitality from 20% to 10%, a sector-specific relief that would bring the sales tax on the sector in line with that in many European countries.
However, critics have said this would be an inefficient way to spur growth and would cost more than £10bn, much of which would benefit large, profitable multinational chains.
A government spokesperson said: “The chancellor prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues – saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year. This is on top of providing a tax break on poured pints and capping corporation tax.”

items.body:
Pets at Home has announced that its Pet Pals programme has now educated more than one million children across the UK, marking a significant milestone in the retailer’s long-standing commitment to improving pet welfare through education.
The achievement follows another successful year for the programme, with 132,303 children attending Pet Pals workshops across six campaigns between Summer 2025 and Summer 2026. During that period, more than 184,000 places were booked across 51,801 sessions held in Pets at Home stores nationwide.
This summer alone, 44,403 children have already attended workshops across 396 stores, with event days still to run and thousands of bookings yet to be recorded, meaning the final attendance figure is expected to increase further.
Pet Pals provides free educational workshops for children aged four to ten, helping them learn the fundamentals of responsible pet ownership through interactive games, activities and hands-on experiences. Topics include nutrition, exercise, grooming, play, friendship and creating suitable environments for pets.
The latest results also highlight growing engagement from families. More households booked workshops during Summer 2026 than in Summer 2025, while attendance rates have improved significantly. The proportion of registered children attending sessions has increased from 69% in Summer 2025 to 75% in Summer 2026, demonstrating stronger participation and engagement.
Dr Samantha Butler-Davies MRCVS, Veterinary Director at Pets at Home, said: “Reaching one million children educated through Pet Pals is an incredible milestone and one that everyone involved in the programme is enormously proud of.
“For many children, Pet Pals provides their first opportunity to learn what it means to care responsibly for an animal. By making pet welfare education fun, interactive and accessible, we’re helping to inspire the next generation of pet owners and giving families the knowledge they need to help pets live happy, healthy lives.
“The continued growth of the programme, and the increasing number of children attending our workshops, highlights the importance of educating young people about responsible pet care. We’re delighted that so many families continue to engage with Pet Pals, helping us extend our positive impact on pet welfare in communities across the UK.”
Since its launch, Pet Pals has become one of the UK’s largest pet welfare education initiatives, with workshops delivered by trained Pets at Home colleagues in stores across the country.
The programme forms part of Pets at Home’s wider commitment to responsible pet ownership, providing children with practical knowledge about caring for animals while encouraging positive relationships between pets and their families.

items.body:
UK readership of articles related to Tesco Clubcard has increased by 1,876% over the last 30 days compared with the preceding 30-day period, as shoppers risk losing £11m worth of Clubcard vouchers.
Data from Taboola’s Newsroom, which captures readership behaviour across the platform’s national publisher network, shows that Clubcard-related articles generated more than 335,000 page views across Taboola’s UK publisher network during the period, up from approximately 17,000 in the previous 30 days.
The approaching expiry of £11 million worth of Clubcard vouchers is the clearest driver of this surge. Coverage from consumer, national and retail publishers – including The Independent and Daily Star – has warned shoppers that affected vouchers will become invalid after 11.59pm on 31st August. Articles have encouraged consumers to check the Tesco app or website and explore their options before their rewards lose their value.
Other Clubcard developments have added to the momentum. These include the return of Clubcard Challenges, through which selected customers can earn up to 5,000 bonus points by completing personalised shopping goals; Tesco’s “Know What You’re Sitting On” campaign highlighting the value of unused rewards; and promotional activity such as the OVO Clubcard Millionaire prize draw.
“Publishers remain among the most trusted places consumers turn when a loyalty scheme can make a tangible difference to their household finances,” said Dave Struzzi, communications lead at Taboola. “Their reporting explains how to get greater value from loyalty programmes, discounts and everyday spending.
“This extraordinary increase in readership also demonstrates that Clubcard has become a powerful consumer brand in its own right. Expiring vouchers, new challenges and rewards campaigns each create fresh news moments for Tesco, keeping Clubcard at the centre of conversations about savings and value while generating significant earned-media attention for the wider Tesco brand.”
