items.body:
For readers who may not be familiar with TFWA, what is its role within the global retail industry?
TFWA is a not-for-profit organisation that brings together the global duty free & travel retail industry. Our members span brands, retailers, airports, airlines, cruise and ferry operators, border stores and other stakeholders across the travel ecosystem, and our role is to provide platforms for connection, insight and business development.
Travel retail is a distinctive part of the wider retail landscape because its customers are uniquely travellers. People are moving between countries, markets and cultures, often with time to explore and discover products in a different way from how they would in traditional shops or online. Our industry is a significant global retail channel in its own right: the latest TFWA Handbook puts annual duty-free and travel-retail sales at around $74 billion. Revenue generated by travel retail is an important part of the investment at travel hubs which supports and enables connectivity, business and leisure travel, and brings families and friends together across the globe.
Our flagship event, TFWA World Exhibition & Conference, takes place each year in Cannes, bringing the international travel retail industry together at scale. Exhibitors span categories including beauty, wines and spirits, confectionery and fine food, fashion and accessories, watches, jewellery, electronics, tobacco, gifts and home goods, with many of the world’s leading luxury brands represented. In 2026 this includes the likes of BVLGARI, Campari, Clarins Group, Hermès, Chanel, Estée Lauder, Lindt, Moët Hennessy and Zegna. At the same time, the exhibition provides an important launchpad for emerging brands and new categories, from digital-native beauty brand Cocunat and wearable technology company HiFuture to premium Italian food brand Bio Orto and innovative Scottish whisky producer InchDairnie. This breadth reflects the changing nature of travel retail, where discovery and newness are becoming increasingly important alongside established global names.
TFWA also organises the TFWA Asia Pacific Exhibition & Conference in Singapore, which brings together a similarly broad range of categories and brands, and throughout the year TFWA provides insight-led research and activities. Across everything we do, our aim is to understand changing traveller behaviour, evolving market conditions and new commercial opportunities, and create platforms that help businesses respond to new trends and grow.
How does travel retail differ from traditional high-street or domestic retail?
Travel retail is a markedly different environment from traditional retail, because almost every aspect of the customer journey is shaped by the fact that people are travelling. You have a captive audience, but also one that is time-sensitive, often navigating an unfamiliar environment and thinking very differently about what they want to buy.
The operating model is different too. Airports are complex, highly regulated environments, with security requirements, restricted deliveries, extended trading hours and significant operating costs. Retailers and brands also have to work within a concession model alongside airport operators, and other stakeholders, so there are more layers involved than you would typically find in shopping centres or on the high street.
At the same time, that creates a unique opportunity. Travel brings together an extraordinary concentration of consumers from different countries, cultures and spending profiles. People are often more open to discovery, gifting and treating their loved ones and themselves when they travel, which gives brands an opportunity to engage customers in ways that are difficult to replicate elsewhere.
Travel retail isn’t simply a high-street store transplanted into an airport or similar transport hub. In an increasingly digital world, travel retail provides a genuine touch point where customers can physically see, smell and taste a wide range of fabulous products, beautifully packaged and highly giftable, at attractive prices.
What can the wider retail sector learn from the way consumers shop while travelling?
Travel provides a particularly interesting retail environment because the consumer is already in a different mindset. They may have more time to browse, are exposed to international brands which they may not find on their local high street and often are looking for products that connect with the destination or the experience of travelling.
The challenge for travel retail is to ensure that the offer is compelling enough to become a meaningful part of the journey, rather than simply another point of purchase.
This is particularly relevant to younger travellers, who are looking for experiences that feel authentic, local and shareable. That has implications for everything from product development and store design to storytelling and the categories that retailers choose to present.
What are travellers looking for from retailers today, and how is that changing?
Travellers increasingly want more than transactional shopping. They want retail experiences that feel engaging, distinctive and relevant to their journey. Authenticity is particularly important, with younger consumers showing a strong interest in experiences that reflect the destination and offer something they cannot find elsewhere. Earlier TFWA research found that 49% of beauty shoppers valued the opportunity to own something unavailable elsewhere.
This is encouraging a shift towards more immersive retail environments, from interactive brand experiences to spaces that bring together shopping, dining, relaxation and local culture. There is a growing opportunity to make retail part of the overall travel experience, rather than something that sits separately from it.
At the same time, travellers expect the same levels of convenience and immediacy they experience in everyday retail. Frictionless journeys and seamless digital services are increasingly important. Smarter use of data can help retailers understand different traveller profiles and anticipate what customers may want, while technologies such as mobile ordering, digital navigation and streamlined checkout can remove points of friction.
What does the future of travel retail look like to you?
I see an industry that will continue to evolve significantly, but one with strong fundamentals. The next few years will require resilience and a willingness to adapt. The opportunity is to become even more relevant to the traveller. That means understanding changing passenger profiles, making better use of technology and data and creating retail experiences that people actively want to engage with.
It also requires collaboration. The industry is interconnected, with brands and retailers highly dependent on the locations in which they operate – airports, cruise ships and other similar stakeholders. None of us can respond effectively to a changing travel environment in isolation.
Ultimately, travel retail has a distinctive proposition. It sits at the crossroads of retail, travel and experience, and it reaches consumers from multiple markets and cultures. The challenge, and the opportunity, is to make that proposition as relevant and compelling as possible for the traveller of the future.

items.body:
One of France’s best-loved premium dessert brands, Brittany based and family-run Marie Morin, has secured its first UK retail listing, with its signature Traditional Chocolate Mousse now available in 300 Marks & Spencer stores across the country.
The launch marks an important milestone for the Breton business, which has been producing premium chilled desserts since 1992. Well known in France for its authentic recipes and commitment to quality, Marie Morin is introducing British shoppers to the product that has become synonymous with the brand – its iconic chocolate mousses.
Marie Morin’s Traditional Chocolate Mousse (2 x 100g) is made using just three ingredients: pure cocoa butter chocolate, free range eggs and salted butter. Presented in distinctive glass jars, the mousse reflects the brand’s authentic, homemade approach to dessert making. Made without colouring agents or preservatives, the mousse delivers a rich chocolate flavour and smooth texture that reflects the simplicity of a homemade recipe.
The recipe highlights the company’s commitment to using carefully selected, high-quality ingredients, chosen to deliver the flavour and texture expected from a premium dessert. This ingredient-led approach is central to the brand, with traditional methods remaining at the heart of its desserts and helping to create products that have built Marie Morin’s reputation in France.
This focus on quality and traditional recipes is rooted in the company’s Breton heritage, where local sourcing plays an important role across the wider Marie Morin range. In particular, the company sources its milk from farms located just a few miles from its production site, helping to ensure freshness and exceptional quality while supporting local agriculture.
Marie Morin was founded by Marie and Alain Morin, whose passion for traditional recipes, regional ingredients and home cooking continues to shape the business today. Now led by the second generation of the Morin family, the company continues to grow while remaining true to its original values.
David Morin, in charge of the UK Development at Marie Morin and a member of the founding family said “Our family has always believed that the best desserts are made with simple, high-quality ingredients and recipes that stay true to tradition. Expanding beyond France has long been an ambition for us, and launching in the UK is an exciting milestone. To secure a listing with Marks & Spencer from the outset is phenomenal, particularly as it only lists a select few outside brands in each category. M&S is renowned for its commitment to quality, making it the ideal partner for our Traditional Chocolate Mousse. We are delighted that British shoppers can now discover a dessert that has been loved in France for generations.”
Marie Morin will be exhibiting at SIAL Paris (17-21 October 2026), where visitors can discover its range of authentic chilled desserts and learn more about the brand.

items.body:
John Lewis has revealed its new in-store restaurant concept in full for the first time, with the opening of the flagship Platter at Oxford Street.
Platter will replace John Lewis restaurants across 32 stores, from Exeter to Edinburgh, by the end of 2027, with Bluewater, Chichester and Reading already reopened. The programme forms part of an £800m multi-year investment in John Lewis.
Platter Oxford Street is the fullest expression of John Lewis’ new restaurant concept, with an open kitchen serving hand-stretched pizza, a made-on-site deli, a dessert parlour, a stylish bar overlooking the shop’s atrium and fifty outdoor covers on the fifth-floor terrace, above Britain’s busiest highstreet. With seating for 300, Platter is one of the biggest restaurants on Oxford Street.
The flagship Platter at Oxford Street will feature a new in-store Roastery. A Master Roaster will oversee the roasting of a single-origin Arabica bean coffee, sourced exclusively for John Lewis, to serve at the Oxford Street site. The coffee will also be available to buy and take home, both as beans and ground coffee bags.
It also houses The Residency, a rotating pop-up launching with London patisserie The Eclectic Collection, whose viral fruit-shaped desserts are available nowhere else outside their own two shops.
Changing consumer trends
The change reflects how differently people shop now. Hospitality accounts for more than 20% of John Lewis in-store transactions and sales have grown by nearly 10% in the past year, as customers spend longer in shops and increasingly treat eating as part of the trip rather than a break from it.
John Lewis opened its first cafe in 1965 and now has 62 cafes and restaurants across the country.
Customer favourites remain across the estate, including scones and fish and chips, and My John Lewis member benefits such as free hot drinks and cake. The restaurants are operated in partnership with Benugo, building on a ten-year relationship.
Each Platter is designed around the scale and character of its shop, so what customers find will vary by location.
Katie Papakonstantinou, Director of Services and Hospitality for John Lewis, said: “This is a real investment in something customers told us mattered. Sitting down for something to eat and drink has become part of how people shop and Platter is built for that.
“Platter serves our own coffee – with beans roasted right here in Oxford Street – alongside an open kitchen making pizza, deli and patisserie on site. Whether stopping for coffee, a pizza with family, a treat from the dessert parlour or a drink at the bar, we’ve created a space that makes a shopping trip even more special.”
Inside Platter John Lewis Oxford Street
- An in-house coffee roastery: overseen by a Master Roaster, the unique bean will be used in Platter’s drinks, with the coffee also available for customers to buy and enjoy at home.
- An open kitchen serving fresh pizza from hand-stretched dough, prepared in front of customers
- A made-on-site deli with freshly prepared salads, cold meats and fish, and grab-and-go options
- A dessert parlour with a full sundae menu, Belgian waffles and a chocolate tap
- Fifty outdoor covers on the fifth-floor terrace, looking across the London skyline
- A stylish bar overlooking the shop’s atrium. With marble counters and dark green leather interiors, it will serve cocktails like hibiscus margaritas and negronis, champagne and bar snacks including charcuterie, cheeseboards and truffle and parmesan fries
- The Residency, a rotating pop-up with exciting premium brands, opening with The Eclectic Collection, known for their fruit shaped desserts.
Platter Oxford Street will sit alongside the retailer’s wider hospitality offer, which includes Benugo, Ori Caffè, Huffkins tea rooms, Jamie Oliver Cafe, the 1864 Rooftop and Kamakura at Oxford Street.
Investment in John Lewis shops
The Platter programme is part of an £800m multi-year investment in the retailer’s shops and digital experience. This summer John Lewis announced £50m across five shops, including a £20m refurbishment of John Lewis Glasgow – its largest single-shop investment in recent years – alongside Cambridge, Leicester, Reading and Liverpool.

Pukka, the nation’s number one pie brand, is set to transform the pie aisle once again as it unveils its biggest brand redesign yet across its entire chilled pie range.
The complete visual overhaul replaces Pukka’s orange packs with powerful recipe-specific colours, creating an unmistakable distinctive new look, designed to stand out at fixture. It also makes favourites easier to find and brings clearer navigation to the category. Pukka’s iconic logo continues to shine through as an orange beacon to the pie aisle, but now the new packs make it easy for shoppers to pick their favourite recipe, with Pukka’s rainbow of foils now also taking centre stage.
Six years ago, Pukka’s move to fully orange boxes revolutionised the pie aisle – marking its transition to more sustainable packaging, with the removal of its plastic windows – helping propel the brand through a period of significant growth. Since then, Pukka’s retail sales have grown from £62m[3] to £82.5m[4] – an increase of 33% – as the brand has expanded its audience and grown distribution. Now, Pukka is using its scale and leadership position to drive the category forward once again.
The redesign puts Pukka’s most powerful brand and product cues front and centre. Every pack is built around three bold elements – a supersized Pukka logo, a generous and appetite-driving image of Pukka’s iconic pie, and distinctive recipe-specific coloured boxes that shoppers will already know and love from Pukka’s unmistakable rainbow of coloured foils. Together, these create maximum impact and excitement at fixture, making Pukka instantly recognisable as the brand revolutionising the category.
Pukka’s iconic orange logo creates a strong, instantly familiar brand block, while its distinctive coloured foils now extend across the entire pack, giving every recipe its own identity. Shoppers can immediately distinguish All Steak in black, Minced Beef & Onion in red and Cheese, Leek & Potato in green, while still recognising each as unmistakably Pukka.
As always, Pukka wanted to ensure the new packaging received a positive response from the nation. Following extensive consumer research and testing, the final design was liked by a massive 85% of respondents[5].
Isaac Fisher, CEO at Pukka, says: “This is a landmark moment for Pukka. Six years ago, we transformed the pie aisle with our orange packaging and built one of the most distinctive brand blocks in the category. Now, we’re ready to drive it forward again with a completely new design that brings even more confidence, colour and impact to the fixture, proudly reflecting our status as one of the category’s most recognisable brands.
“People know exactly what to expect from Pukka – iconic, great quality pies packed with full-on flavour. Our new design captures that confidence with a giant Pukka logo front and centre, a big, delicious-looking pie, and bold coloured packs inspired by our rainbow of foils, providing distinction between recipes. Nothing gets lost. Nothing competes for attention.
“Pukka orange optimism continues to shine through. Our iconic logo is now bigger and bolder than ever, creating a powerful Pukka block across the fixture. Shoppers love being able to spot their Pukka favourites through the coloured foils, so we’ve put these recipe colours at the heart of the design so they can find their favourites at a glance – much like they would navigate the crisp aisle.”
The redesign now also sees black text against a white background on the back of packs, improving readability and making it easier for shoppers to easily navigate ingredients and nutritional information, while clearer cooking instructions create a more seamless journey from pie aisle to plate.
Each recipe will also carry its own QR code, another pioneering feature from Pukka, that will give shoppers easy access to additional product information and help prepare the range for the future evolution of on-pack barcodes.
The new identity will extend far beyond packaging, rippling through Pukka’s wider brand plans and creating a bold, cohesive look wherever shoppers experience it. Major activation plans will support the launch and drive further excitement around the brand, with more details set to be revealed soon.
Fisher concludes: “This is the start of a big new chapter for Pukka. The packs will make an immediate impact, but they’re only the beginning. We have ambitious plans to bring the new identity to life, create more reasons for shoppers to choose Pukka and drive even more energy, colour and full-on flavour to the category, like only Pukka can.”
Pukka’s new-look chilled pie range will begin rolling into supermarkets towards the end of August, available in 205g packs at an RRP of £2.25. The full range will also be available across wholesale and convenience.

items.body:
LOOKFANTASTIC has unveiled its A/W ’26 Trend Report, an insider guide to the beauty movements already gaining momentum and set to shape the season ahead.
Powered by digital trend intelligence, LOOKFANTASTIC platform data and insights from TikTok, Reddit, Content Creators, industry experts and LOOKFANTASTIC’s Buying team, the report goes beyond predicting the next viral moment. Instead, it identifies the cultural and consumer shifts changing the way beauty is discovered, understood and experienced.
From a renewed focus on skin health and prevention to the continued evolution of K- Beauty, the rise of scalp-first haircare and a return to bold self-expression, the A/W ’26 beauty landscape is being shaped by a consumer who wants more from their beauty with the defining shift for A/W ’26 being intentionality.
LOOKFANTASTIC Managing Director, Keely Gough explains:
Staying ahead is not about chasing trends, but understanding the shifts changing how consumers discover, shop and experience beauty. With an increasingly complex landscape of recommendations, viral moments and evolving routines, trusted expertise is becoming more important than ever.
This shift is also being reflected in how consumers are discovering and choosing beauty, with trust, peer recommendations and considered decision-making increasingly influencing the path to purchase.
Lore Oxford, Head of Insights Product, Reddit noted:
We’ve entered a new era of beauty discovery where recommendations and peer reviews are the ultimate currency…This rise in engagement reflects a broader shift in how people make beauty decisions, with shoppers seeking authentic, peer-led recommendations from a community of like-minded enthusiasts.
1. Skin Barrier 2.0
Skin Barrier 2.0 marks a move away from treating skin concerns reactively towards futureproofing skin health. Now ranking as LOOKFANTASTIC’s fifth-highest skin concern, on-site search activity is up +28.5%, with three-year growth reaching +182%. Meanwhile, once specialist skincare terms ceramides and postbiotics have seen +419% search growth on TikTok over the last year.
The focus is shifting towards targeted formulas that support the skin’s natural defences, with barrier-building lipids, microbiome-friendly ferments and restorative actives taking centre stage.
2. Skin Streaming
Last year’s elaborate routines are giving way to a more efficient approach. Skin streaming reflects a consumer who has become increasingly knowledgeable about ingredients and unwilling to use products simply for the sake of another step. Instead, consumers reach for multi-tasking formulas that deliver more from fewer products are earning permanent places in beauty cabinets.
SPF is emerging as a hero of this streamlined approach, combining protection with additional skincare or makeup benefits. From Beauty of Joseon’s Relief Sun Rice + Probiotics SPF50+ to Quick Flick’s Quick Screen Setting Spray SPF50+, multifunctionality is becoming a key part of the new beauty routine.
As Content Creator Natalie O’Neill puts it, consumers are becoming “much wiser” and “far pickier” when it comes to their routines — simultaneously reducing the number of products they use while increasing their understanding of what each product does.
3. Beauty Longevity
The anti-ageing conversation is evolving and rather than focusing solely on reversing visible signs of ageing, beauty longevity is centred around maintaining healthy-looking skin over time with prevention, regeneration and resilience becoming the new priorities.
Searches for longevity-related skincare at LOOKFANTASTIC are up +4.7% quarter-on- quarter, reflecting growing interest in long-term skin health rather than quick, visible fixes.
An ingredient at the forefront is PDRN, with LOOKFANTASTIC searches accelerating +54% QoQ, while TikTok data shows #PDRN has experienced a remarkable +990.91% growth over three years. Retinal searches are also up +26.2% QoQ, while TikTok growth has reached 4,837% since 2023.
The movement is also moving beyond topical skincare. Sales of skin electrical tools at LOOKFANTASTIC have risen +101.3% YoY, signalling growing consumer appetite for beauty technology that brings more advanced treatments into the home.
As Dr Jonquille Chantrey notes in the report, the future of aesthetic medicine is moving away from age reversal towards healthy prejuvenation and visible biological health.
4. K-Beauty
K-Beauty has moved beyond viral curiosity and into purchase confidence with TikTok searches for #KBeauty up +719% since 2023. Meanwhile, K-Beauty sales at LOOKFANTASTIC have grown +158% YoY, with skincare accounting for 80% of the category.
The movement is also generating significant engagement beyond TikTok, with UK views to Reddit’s r/AsianBeauty reaching 5.8 million and r/KoreanBeauty reaching 730,000 in the first six months of 2026.
But the next phase of K-Beauty is about more than “glass skin”. Consumers are increasingly seeking targeted ingredients and formulations that address concerns including dryness, sun damage, ageing and compromised skin barriers.
Niacinamide, PDRN, peptides and collagen are all delivering triple-digit growth, according to LOOKFANTASTIC Senior Buying Manager Lauren Starkey, while probiotics are emerging as another ingredient to watch.
5. Beauty & Wellness
The crossover between beauty and wellness is accelerating, with consumers embracing a more holistic approach encompassing nutrition, recovery, stress, hormone balance and overall wellbeing.
At LOOKFANTASTIC, wellness-related product sales are up +28% YoY, while collagen is growing +6.8% QoQ and supplements and vitamins remain a high-performing segment, with a 20% conversion rate. The result is a more integrated beauty routine, with customers increasingly purchasing wellness products alongside their skincare and haircare essentials.
As LOOKFANTASTIC Senior Buying Manager Lauren Starkey explains, the longevity movement is ultimately part of a broader mindset centred on self-care, prevention and a more holistic approach to health and wellbeing.
6. The Hair Growth Revolution
For A/W ’26, the scalp is becoming the new focus of haircare, with consumers increasingly treating the scalp with the same level of attention as facial skin.
Related terms including “scalp treatment”, “scalp scrub” and “dry scalp” have generated more than 4,111 LOOKFANTASTIC searches, while the hair loss and growth category is up +37% YoY.
The shift is also moving consumers towards complete, routine-led solutions. Searches for “hair growth” and related terms generated 18,789 searches in the last quarter, while products associated with growth and thickening benefits have risen +15.9% YoY and products tagged to the “Growth and Thickening” trend have accelerated +42%.
As LOOKFANTASTIC Buying Manager Beth Eyre explains, customers are increasingly buying into full routines, with routine-led bundles becoming a key area of growth.
7. Maximalist Makeup is Back
After years of pared-back aesthetics, more is more is making its return. The A/W ’26 beauty consumer is moving away from prescriptive aesthetics and towards looks that feel authentic, individual and personal by embracing colour, texture and statement details.
Searches for brows are up +25.3%, eyes +19.3% and lips +11.7%, signalling renewed appetite for the features that allow consumers to define and personalise their look.
LOOKFANTASTIC Expert and Makeup Artist Jeyanney is seeing the same shift professionally, noting a growing demand for more polished, glamorous looks with greater definition, structure and impact.
But maximalism doesn’t necessarily mean heavy coverage. As the report puts it: “Less coverage, more character.”
8. Bronzer is Back
Alongside maximalist makeup, one beauty staple is reclaiming its place in the spotlight: bronzer.
Drawing on the continued popularity of skin-first aesthetics, A/W ’26 is embracing a more relaxed, lived-in approach to complexion, with soft definition and healthy-looking radiance replacing heavy contouring.
Fake tan sales at LOOKFANTASTIC are up +21.5%, bronzers are up +5.1%, and brown shades have grown +10.4% YoY.
The movement is also evolving through “skinified” self-tan, with formulas increasingly incorporating ingredients such as peptides and niacinamide alongside bronzing benefits.
9. Fragrance as Identity
Perhaps nowhere is personalisation more apparent than fragrance. The traditional idea of finding one signature scent is giving way to the fragrance wardrobe — a collection of scents chosen according to mood, personality, occasion and season.
UK views of Reddit’s r/perfumesthatfeellikesthis have grown by more than +60% over the last six months, reflecting growing appetite for fragrance discovery and experimentation. Meanwhile, fragrance sets at LOOKFANTASTIC increased +13% in H1 2026 compared with the same period last year.
Layering is expected to continue growing as consumers experiment with combining scents to create their own individual fragrance identity.
While vanilla remains the most in-demand note, cherry is the fragrance profile to watch, with searches up +16% YoY and a 13% conversion rate. Pistachio is another standout note, with searches up +29.8% QoQ and a 12.5% conversion rate.
Hair perfume is also breaking away from the traditional fragrance format, with sales up +71% YoY as consumers expand their scent wardrobes beyond eau de parfum.
The New Season of Beauty
Across skincare, haircare, makeup, fragrance and wellness, the A/W ’26 trends point towards the same fundamental shift: beauty consumers are becoming more informed, more intentional and more individual.
They are streamlining rather than accumulating. Investing in prevention rather than correction. Looking to science and technology for smarter solutions. Treating beauty as part of wider wellbeing. And, at the same time, embracing colour, creativity and personal expression.
The result is a beauty landscape that is both more considered and more expressive — where there is no single definition of what is “in”.

A "social supermarket" offering low-cost food and support to escape financial hardship is to open at a third location in Kent.
SE Kitchen is due to open at the Pentagon Shopping Centre in Chatham in October, adding to branches in Ashford and Ramsgate.
The food shops, run by Social Enterprise Kent, redistribute surplus food and offer cut-price groceries.

Teresa Murray, the council's deputy leader, said access to affordable and healthy food was "critically important" and a key factor in people's well-being.

items.body:
The national lottery is facing questions over its new boss’s record in the gambling industry, including a lucrative role in the 24-hour slot machine sector singled out by the prime minister as a blight on British high streets.
Allwyn UK, which holds a licence to run the Lottery until 2034, said last week that it had appointed William Hill’s former UK and Ireland boss Phil Walker as its interim chief executive, replacing Andria Vidler.
While Walker may not get the job on a permanent basis, MPs have written to the Gambling Commission, the industry regulator, about his selection as a steward of the UK’s most high-profile gambling brand, given the lottery’s “unique position” in public life.
In a letter seen by the Guardian, Labour’s Dawn Butler and Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith told the regulator they were “deeply concerned” by the appointment.
They cited a personal sanction the regulator imposed on Walker in 2024 over “widespread and alarming” failures to enforce money laundering and terrorist financing controls at William Hill, which was fined a record £19.2m the previous year.
They also raised concerns about a boardroom role he holds with Game Nation, the UK’s third-largest chain of adult gaming centres (AGCs).
AGCs are high street gambling venues that are often referred to as “slot farms” due to their high concentration of slot machines, and are open 24 hours a day in most cases.
Last year, upon taking a job with City Gaming Ltd, which owns Game Nation, Walker said he was excited to “develop and grow [the company] over the coming years”.
That view appears to put the industry veteran at odds with the government, just as he prepares to take the reins of the lottery, frequently described as the UK’s largest public sector contract, worth £6.5bn in revenue over 10 years.
While still mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham hit out at AGCs, accusing the sector of “targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities”.
This month, he announced plans to tighten up the permissive licensing regime that has allowed the sector to achieve the growth Walker has previously advocated for.
Butler, who was instrumental in Burnham’s decision to crack down on AGCs, has written to the Gambling Commission raising concerns about the appointment.
In a letter co-signed by Duncan Smith she said the pair were seeking clarity on whether Walker’s work for City Gaming was “compatible” with the decision to select him to run the lottery.
With regard to his tenure at William Hill, they asked the regulator to “explain what consideration, if any, was given to this history when assessing his suitability for his present position”.
A Gambling Commission spokesperson said: “We would not publicly comment on an operator’s personnel decisions.”
Jackie Olden, a campaigner whose terminally ill mother lost thousands of pounds to Merkur, the AGC sector’s second-largest company, also questioned Walker’s suitability to run the lottery, played by about 20 million people on a regular basis.
“It’s awful that someone heavily involved with 24-hour slot farms that destroy families and communities can run the country’s biggest public sector contract,” she said.
Companies House filings indicate that Walker is likely to have earned more than £50,000 from his non-executive directorship with Game Nation, a role that typically requires attendance at a small number of board meetings each year.
On Tuesday, Game Nation said that Walker would “step back” from his role with the company, with effect from 1 September, for the duration of his interim contract with the national lottery.
A spokesperson for Allwyn said: “As we navigate an increasingly competitive environment, Phil Walker brings valuable operational, digital and marketing experience alongside a significant understanding of our operating landscape.
“His appointment will help deliver the next stage of growth and innovation of the national lottery, and we look forward to welcoming Phil to the role of interim CEO.”
Allwyn, which is ultimately owned by the Czech billionaire Karel Komárek, has previously highlighted that Walker did not lose his personal licence from the Gambling Commission over the sanction imposed while at William Hill, indicating that the regulator believes him fit and proper to run a business in the sector.
The national lottery is regulated separately from the rest of the gambling sector. It is run under a 10-year licence from the Gambling Commission and mandated to donate billions of pounds to good causes.
By contrast, City Gaming is owned by investors in a “tactical value” fund, run by the Wall Street bank Morgan Stanley.
Last year, an employment tribunal judge heard a case of unfair dismissal brought by a former employee of its Game Nation chain.
According to a witness statement submitted during the case, a customer who disliked the staff member once paid a homeless man to defecate on the floor of the shop toilet, so that she was forced to clear it up.
Game Nation was ordered to pay the staff member £6,598.44, albeit for a technicality related to its dismissal procedure rather than the incident. Based on its £32m revenues last year, the company made the money back in less than two hours.
The Guardian has approached the government for comment.

items.title: Back to school: How to save on uniform costs
items.summary: From baby banks to supermarket deals, there are many ways parents can ease the back-to-school burden.
items.body:
Back to school: How parents can save on uniform costs
- Published
Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs it brings.
Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.
And a third of the 2,000 parents polled said they've sacrificed things for themselves to meet back-to-school costs like uniforms, bags or books.
New rules limiting the number of items branded with a school logo to three per child come into force in September, aimed at helping ease the financial burden.
From baby banks to council grants, here are ways parents can ease the cost of kitting out their kids for school.
Your first port of call
Save the Children said the new uniform rules are a "good start" but back-to-school costs remain a concern for families across almost all income brackets.
The government said schools should make second-hand uniforms accessible to parents.
"Speak to a teacher you trust, and explain that the costs are difficult," said Megan Meek-O'Connor, head of England and Westminster at Save the Children.
Many schools have uniform hubs, swap shops and sales just before term starts, and hardship funds.
In London, the School Uniform Reuse Network launched earlier this year, giving schools practical advice to start or improve their own swap shops.
During its first term of operation, it saw more than 1,500 items reused across 24 schools.
Don't dismiss baby banks
Parents of older children may not realise a so-called baby bank can help them, but many of the 400 support hubs across the UK provide uniforms for children up to and through secondary school.
In its latest survey of members, the Baby Bank Alliance found school uniform was reported as a priority item for the first time.
Late summer is one of the busiest times for Little Stars Shrewsbury - just over half the children helped since June have been given uniform support.
Hannah Stoddart, operations manager at Little Stars Shrewsbury, said families come to them in varying circumstances. A child starting school might need fully kitting out, while an older pupil may just need to replace one or two items.
Stoddart stressed that while the summer holidays "take their toll", the charity provides help all year.
"So when they've had that growth spurt, when they've scuffed their shoes or they've ripped their trousers or they need a winter coat, that's something they can come back to us for as well," she said.
Supermarkets and pre-loved items
The relaxed rules on uniform branding mean parents can purchase more items from supermarkets and charity shops, said Save the Children's Meek-O'Connor.
Pre-loved items are usually what "kids have grown out of quickly rather than things that are poor quality", she said.
Parents can cheaply stock up on frequent-wear items with supermarket bundle deals, while the charity Family Action suggested they team up to bulk buy items that would otherwise take them over budget.
According to research from the bank Nationwide, a third of parents said they buy uniform from supermarkets, a third shop around for the best value and 23% purchase larger sizes so items last longer.
Kate Steere, parent and consumer editor at the comparison site Finder, said sports kit costs can be "brutal".
"I always encourage parents to tap into their club's community. Families with older kids are usually eager to pass down gear," she said.
"My boys' football team runs a summer sale for second-hand kit, and apps like Vinted or Facebook Marketplace are goldmines."
Check for council grants
You may be able to get a grant from your local authority if your income is below a certain threshold or you're receiving certain benefits.
These can be worth up to Â£200 per child.
Eligibility and how much you can get can vary according to where in the UK you live, so it is best to check with your council directly.
Struggling with uniform costs is common and people shouldn't feel ashamed if they need to ask for help, said Meek-O'Connor.
"Uniform is supposed to be about making school kind of more accessible, more equal... it should be something positive," she said.

items.body:
Lancashire has been the site of many British innovations throughout history, from the spinning jenny, which transformed textile production, to the creation of jelly babies.
Now it has welcomed another first: AI shopping trolleys.
A Morrisons in Lancashire has become the first supermarket in the UK to trial the use of “smart trolleys” that allow customers to do their shopping without having to scan a single item.
The AI-powered Caper smart trolleys, created by San Francisco-based Instacart, automatically register each item placed in the trolley, adding up the cost and recommending related products as you shop. Once finished, customers can scan their trolley screen rather than visiting a checkout.
Preston is the first city in Britain to use them after the supermarket chain announced a deal to trial them at its location in Ashton-on-Ribble, to the west of the city.
Amazon Fresh, which allowed shoppers to take items from the shelves and leave the shop without checking out, using cameras to charge directly to online accounts, failed to take off in the UK, with the company’s last physical British store closing in 2025. But Morrisons is more hopeful that its smart trolleys will be a success, with plans to put them in supermarkets across the country.
The smart trolleys are already used in more than 100 cities across the world. They are similar in design and function to the Dash Cart used by Amazon’s Fresh stores, which still operate outside the UK.
After the trolleys rolled into Ashton-on-Ribble last month, customer Matthew Byrne said they had “massively” helped him keep track of his shopping. Byrne is autistic and struggles to stick to set plans for what to get from the shops.
“Having what I’ve bought on screen has been great. I have a habit of just grabbing things and throwing them in my trolley, and then wondering how I’m paying so much. It’s been amazing to visualise it and see it in real time. I came here with an £80 budget, and I’ve actually been able to stick to it.”
Kaz Bond was disappointed to be forced to use a normal trolley for her latest shop due to a fault on her phone, having used them for every trip she has made to Morrisons since they became commonplace around four weeks ago.
“Honestly, I think they’re brilliant,” said Bond. “They make life much easier. I wouldn’t be that surprised if they’re everywhere before long. I reckon it’s the future.”
Debbie Files had chosen Tuesday as the day to take a leap of faith and use the trolleys for the first time, albeit with the help of a Morrisons employee.
“It was a little bit confusing at first, but you get used to it pretty quickly,” said Files. “It’s heavy, though. I’ve barely been able to turn it. I feel like I need a driving lesson to use it, but I got the hang of it. If they make a smaller one then that will get me to use it again.”

items.title: The Danish retailer plotting to outsmart ‘unsentimental’ Modella Capital
items.summary: On the modern-day British high street, a Scandinavian shop featuring maze-like aisles, quirky homeware and bags of licorice near the till is not quite a reinvention of the wheel.  But Mikkel Grene, chief executive of Danish homeware retailer Søstrene Grene, believes his business can go toe-to-toe with Ikea and Flying Tiger for pride of place [...]
items.body:
The Danish retailer plotting to outsmart ‘unsentimental’ Modella Capital
On the modern-day British high street, a Scandinavian shop featuring maze-like aisles, quirky homeware and bags of licorice near the till is not quite a reinvention of the wheel.
But Mikkel Grene, chief executive of Danish homeware retailer Søstrene Grene, believes his business can go toe-to-toe with Ikea and Flying Tiger for pride of place in the living rooms and kitchens of UK shoppers.
Flying Tiger, which Grene concedes is seen as his closest competitor, was snapped up by private equity firm Modella Capital in May.
This year, Modella drew criticism for pushing through a drastic restructuring of TG Jones – the former high street arm of WH Smith – and oversaw the collapse of Claire’s Accessories.
Though Modella is yet to launch a restructuring of Flying Tiger in the UK, Grene tells City AM that Søstrene Grene has already begun taking over a number of stores vacated by its Danish rival in two other markets.
He would consider opening stores in former Flying Tiger sites in Britain too, he says. “We’ll just look at these units as any other unit. It will just be another unit for us because we don’t see Flying Tiger as a competitor, really, because we have such a different offering.” Flying Tiger declined to comment.
Family ownership key for Søstrene Grene
Grene is keen to emphasise that he doesn’t view Flying Tiger and Søstrene Grene as comparable, because the latter is family-owned. Grene’s parents founded the business in 1973 and his brother Cresten serves as its creative director.
Being family-owned allows the retailer to “think long term” and “leaves room for all the whimsical and non-commercial things that we do,” he says.
This is a sharp comparison to Modella, Grene says: “[They] are going to be quite unsentimental, these new owners. It’s going to be a big question mark whether they are going to work really long term. That remains to be seen.
“What I said about the benefits of our family ownership, I obviously don’t think they have that, but maybe they have something else that we don’t have that they can benefit from.”
One such “non-commercial” move for Søstrene Grene was the opening of its flagship store on Oxford Circus last year. “We knew it was not going to be an easy case, and it was probably not going to be the most profitable store because the rent levels are really high there,” he says.
“But it is the best store in terms of turnover in all of the UK stores. So I’m really happy with it, and it’s more like a flagship store where we want to showcase the brand. So it’s important in that sense to be in these high-traffic locations.”
Before opening in one of the world’s most well-known shopping destinations, Søstrene Grene hunted for lower rents in the outskirts of Britain’s cities. Grene points to Manchester, where the retailer opened in “one of the back streets” before moving to the Arndale, one of the UK’s biggest shopping centres.
E-commerce ‘putting retailers out of business’
Grene says he was surprised by the tax bill facing retailers when the company first expanded into the UK in 2016. Business rates account for as much as 50 per cent of the bill his shops pay to landlords, he said, compared to 10 per cent for the equivalent tax in much of Europe.
“I think that’s probably the main reason why we see so many empty units in London because it’s still [at] a high level. So even though it has come down, it’s still very expensive,” he says.
While Søstrene Grene has become well-known for its low prices, its boss says that his and other retailers are routinely undercut by Chinese e-commerce giants like Shein and Temu.
The government should take action to “level the playing field,” he says. “We have the muscles to battle all this, but we also have small retailers and small players in the UK that are really struggling to compete with this for and for a good reason. There are some companies being put out of business, and is that really fair?”
Shein and Temu did not respond to requests for comment.
The Treasury has acknowledged the damaging impact of “low-value” imports and is set to shut the ‘de-minimis’ loophole – which exempts small parcels from import duties – in October 2028. But retailers have warned that the EU’s crackdown on small imports earlier this month will cause these e-commerce firms to redouble their focus on the UK market.
Søstrene Grene operates about 47 stores in the UK and plans to reach 100 locations next year. The retailer saw pre-tax profit dip one per cent to 213m Danish Krone (£24m) in the year to April 2025, while its turnover jumped by a record 31 per cent to 2.9bn Danish Krone (£327m).
Grene says there is no need for external funding or a public listing despite the retailer’s ambitious expansion plans.
“We’re quite pleased with being a family-owned and operated company,” he says. “I think it gives us some good opportunities to think long term and work long term, and sometimes you need to sacrifice one quarter or one year to be really strong in three years from now.”
The retailer has just completed a “really expensive” overhaul of its back-office systems and a programme to automate most of its warehouse operations, which Grene says were “difficult bets” made easier by the firm’s family ownership.
Taking the retailer out of the hands of the Grene family would force the business to become more “logical,” the chief executive says. “We could definitely streamline Søstrene Grene more as Flying Tiger is doing, as Ikea is doing. But I also think that we will lose something because the whole idea about Søstrene Grene is that it is a bit mysterious, it’s a bit quirky, it’s a bit whimsical.”

items.summary: Coles full-year results show that despite gaining market share over past 12 months, sales fell over four weeks of ‘competitor’s collectables campaign’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Woolworths’ latest Disney “Ooshie” collectibles have not only captivated Australian children, they have led to a short-term slump in competitor Coles’ sales. items.body:
Woolworths’ latest Disney “Ooshie” collectibles have not only captivated Australian children, they have led to a short-term slump in competitor Coles’ sales.
Thousands of shoppers switched supermarkets to collect the plastic figurines, trading them online and in classrooms. Some schools have banned the toys, which can be collected after a customer spends $30, and environmentalists have labelled them “future landfill”.
The latest rubber figurine promotion was scheduled to end on Tuesday, but strong customer interest meant Woolworths prematurely ran out of Ooshies a week ago.
Coles on Tuesday released its full-year results, showing it had grown supermarket sales and gained market share against Woolworths in the 12 months to June.
Growth continued into July but then slumped amid a “competitor’s collectables campaign”, Coles announced.
The Coles chief executive, Leah Weckert, said the moderation in sales was a “temporary impact” lasting nearly four weeks. It mostly affected bricks-and-mortar shops rather than online shopping.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Michael Toner said the impact of the Woolworths campaign could scare Coles investors.
Ooshies, designed to fit on to the top of pens or pencils, come in generic packaging. It is not clear what figure you have received until the pack is ripped open, mostly by keen children who then trade the Ooshies at home or school in an attempt to collect all 40 characters, from Disney, Marvel and Star Wars.
Schoolchildren also stage Ooshie battles where they flick the characters to try to knock down competitors’ figures.
Woolworths has hosted dedicated swap meets across the country in recent weeks to help customers complete their collections.
Adult customers have turned to online marketplaces to trade Ooshies. A dedicated Facebook Ooshie swap group added almost 2,500 members in the past week and now has more than 45,000 members.
The 2019 Ooshies craze culminated in two farmers destroying a rare lion Ooshie live on TV in a protest against online bullying after they tried to sell it. On Tuesday, one eBay listing for an “ultra rare” fuzzy-textured figurine of Bullseye, the Toy Story horse, was set to sell for at least $750. Others are listed for thousands of dollars.
‘Just future landfill’
Prof Gary Mortimer, a consumer behaviour expert at the Queensland University of Technology business school, said Ooshies could help children build social skills – similar to when youngsters traded marbles or Pokémon cards last century.
“That was a part of the social etiquette of learning how to compromise and how to share,” Mortimer said.
“They’re looking for a particular one to complete the set and then negotiating – ‘so I’ll give you two of these for one of those’ – so I do think there’s some social benefits.”
But some schools have moved to shut down trading.
Bellevue Park state school in Queensland posted on Facebook that it had banned Ooshies due to “distractions, conflict and unfair trading”.
“We need your support to make sure these items remain safe at home and are not bought to school where they can become lost, damaged or stolen,” it wrote in a Facebook post.
One Sydney after-school care centre said it was no longer allowing the toys because there had been “disputes around trading and ownership, and situations where children have become upset or distressed”.
The bans are a badge of honour for Alan Ngov, the chief commercial officer at Headstart International, the company that developed Ooshies.
“You know it was a good one when you get banned from the school yard! What an amazing campaign from the Woolworths, Disney and Headstart teams!” he wrote on LinkedIn.
Environmental groups are concerned about the volume of plastic that will eventually end up in landfill. Kirsten Junor, the chief executive of not-for-profit Reverse Garbage, said the carbon emissions used to make and transport Ooshies outweighed any benefit.
“It’s just future landfill,” she said in a video posted on social media earlier this month.
“Kids don’t need them. We don’t need them. The planet doesn’t need them. Stop making them. You don’t need to get a reward every time you go shopping for what you need.”
Woolworths has said Ooshie figures are made from “97% recycled thermoplastic rubber”. The company has offered dedicated collection bins in some stores to recycle the figures.
Nearly two-thirds of parents surveyed by polling company YouGov said they changed their shopping behaviour due to the Ooshies promotion, including shopping at Woolworths more often.
One in five adult Ooshies collectors planned to sell the products online, YouGov’s survey released this week found. Millennials were most keen on collecting them, while baby boomers were interested in passing them on to loved ones.
Weckert said on Tuesday that Coles planned to continue its own promotional collectible campaigns in the future.
Coles reported its net profit rose 1% to $1.09bn in the year to June. Its supermarkets increased their profit margin on earnings from 5.3% to 5.7%.

items.body:
Leicestershire police won’t say who first told them about Jigar Gheewala, but you can see why, once they had heard of him, they decided to find out more. Gheewala was unemployed, had no apparent income, yet lived in a £1.3m house and sent his three children to private school. “He was a declared bankrupt, with a bank account that was absolutely not reflective of what it should be,” said financial crime supervisor Laura Panter of Leicestershire police’s economic crime team. “That was our starting point.”
Over the course of 2020, despite being on benefits, Gheewala’s bank account received more than £880,000 in cash in 200 different deposits. He was, it turned out, a money launderer, but not the kind you’ll see in the movies. Gheewala’s deposits had been made not in Liechtenstein or on Grand Cayman, but at various post office branches in Leicester, one thick wodge of banknotes after another.
As banks have closed branches all over Britain, post offices have quietly become central to how we move our money. In 2017, post offices began to accept deposits on behalf of banks, and those deposits now exceed £30bn a year. The way it works is straightforward. A customer hands over banknotes to be counted, then inserts a bank card and enters the pin, like a cashpoint in reverse. The post office system then communicates with the bank’s system, which credits the value of the cash to the account linked to the card.
It is a simple system, which Post Office Ltd, the state-owned company that controls the branches, says provides a crucial service to businesses and individuals otherwise cut off from banking services. But the simplicity comes at a cost. It has eliminated many of the checks that previously stopped criminals from laundering their cash. In the same way you can use someone else’s card to take money from a cashpoint, provided you know the pin, you can use any bank card to make a deposit at the post office. The process is deliberately streamlined and, unlike at a bank, the post office operative (often referred to as postmaster or subpostmaster) has no way to access any of the account details, and thus no way to check if the person with the card is its holder, or whether this transaction is part of a suspicious pattern.
Law enforcement agencies estimate that, alongside ordinary businesses’ takings, hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being paid into the post office each year. This allows drug dealers and other criminals to bank their illicit wealth, and profit from their crimes, and to do so with the absolute minimum of effort. “The number of places where cash can come into the economy is vast now but, as bank branches continue to close, the number of places to pay it back in has necessarily become more restricted. You’ve got this sort of reverse funnel effect going on,” said a former Post Office employee with knowledge of how it organises financial services. “The bad guys are genuinely targeting post offices as one of the few places left where they can actually go to put money in.”
Leicestershire police used Gheewala’s transactions to reconstruct how he operated. On a typical day, he might make his first cash deposit in the east of the city, at a post-office counter hosted by a convenience store; then it would be a five-minute drive to another store, with boxes of veg out the front, its windows obscured by decals of soft drinks and spirits, offering post office services alongside the scratchcards. A few minutes away was another branch, between a chemist and a fried chicken shop, before another short drive would bring him to a retail centre where the post office sat next to a bakery on a prosperous-looking residential street. A final drive north would take him to a convenience store among red-brick detached houses, and that was a morning’s work done: thousands of pounds deposited in an hour or so, bundles of criminal cash being paid into the most ordinary of locations.
“When we started looking at this, we were then able to see other individuals in Leicestershire that were mimicking exactly the same activity,” said Panter. “What we were finding was there was quite a consistent pattern in terms of the deposit activity around post offices.”
Panter and her colleagues’ investigation became Operation Kilo, which began in 2021 and culminated in December 2025 with Gheewala being sentenced to almost 12 years in prison, along with six co-conspirators. And this was not just a Leicester-based operation. Officers watched as couriers came to Leicester with bags full of cash earned by criminals from London and Yorkshire, stashing them in shops for Gheewala’s people to pick up. Each day’s haul would be distributed among a network of underlings, who trekked around the city’s post offices, paying rubber-band-bound stacks of banknotes into as many as 10 different accounts at each stop, using cards with the pins written on the back.
The bank accounts into which the money was deposited belonged to ordinary people – “mules” in police jargon – who received small payments for renting them out, or to companies in Leicester’s garment business, where managers faked invoices to make the payments look legitimate. (Gheewala promised the mules £50 per £10,000 laundered, but in reality he often seems to have paid them less than that.) Gheewala controlled the whole operation from a laptop kept in an otherwise empty house, with all the account details and their passwords written down in a notebook. As soon as the money appeared online he would, using cryptocurrency exchanges, disperse it around the world.
In two years, Gheewala’s group moved an astonishing £53m, allowing organised criminals to legitimise their earnings on an industrial scale. It’s not clear how much exactly Gheewala was charging for the service, although to judge by the lifestyle he was living, he was doing well out of it.
His operation might have been big, but it wasn’t unique. Just a month after Gheewala’s conviction, two men were jailed in Birmingham for an almost-identical scheme, in which they paid in up to £200,000 a day as they travelled between 10 post offices in the east of the city. In April, a man from Cheltenham was jailed for six years and eight months for controlling a network of mules paying millions of pounds of cash into post offices in Bristol and Gloucestershire.
And this has been going on for a while. Two men were jailed at Southwark crown court in 2024 for paying £26m into post offices in London and Manchester before their arrests in 2017. Students have been jailed in Scotland for paying criminal money into post offices, and there are other ongoing cases in which similar crimes are alleged.
If it wasn’t for what has been going on elsewhere in the Post Office, this would be a major story. Instead, it has been largely ignored.
The Post Office Horizon scandal burst into the public consciousness thanks to 2024’s ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office, but by that stage it had been dragging on for two decades. Post Office Ltd wrongly prosecuted hundreds of its post office operatives, despite senior figures knowing that the computer program that supposedly showed they had been committing fraud was faulty. Ex-post office operative Alan Bates’s landmark victory against his former employers in 2019 forced the government to overturn his and others’ convictions, and to promise to pay hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation.
The scandal is one of Britain’s worst miscarriages of justice. One of its unfortunate side effects is that it has impeded investigations into how much money is being laundered via post office branches. Even if police officers are themselves confident that figures originating in Post Office Ltd’s Horizon software (a version of which is still being used) are reliable, they are aware that many jury members will – for understandable reasons – be intensely sceptical. Documents released by the inquiry into the Horizon scandal show that, in 2024, just a few weeks after the ITV drama was first aired, a detective constable from Blackburn police station decided to halt an investigation into “large-scale money laundering, and possibly other fraud offences” via post office branches in Lancashire out of concern that defence lawyers would find it too easy to discredit evidence originating from the computer system.
“After the Mr Bates TV show, it became a real hot potato and nobody wanted to get hold of it,” said one officer, who asked to remain anonymous. “For every case that’s brought, there are many more in the background. There is no real appetite to do anything unless it’s a slam dunk, because the public is on the side of the post office operatives.” So the problem remains. “It’s the way that you can pay money into the post office without checks, that’s the problem. It’s huge.”
If you look at the raw numbers, you can see his point. In October 2020, cash deposits at post-office branches across the UK totalled £1.9bn. That is £1.9bn for that single month, not the whole year. The following October, the sum was £2.2bn. That number kept rising each year until, by October 2025, it came to £2.9bn – an increase of 50% in just five years. Although Post Office Ltd then stopped publishing such detailed figures, the trend has continued. It boasted of a 10% increase in deposits in the first quarter of this year, meaning they have now almost certainly passed £3bn a month.
What makes these numbers so astounding is that over the same period, cash usage among the general public has dropped sharply. Cash now accounts for fewer than one in 10 transactions in the UK. Yet cash deposits at the post office have gone sharply in the opposite direction.
According to Post Office Ltd, the reason it stopped publishing monthly cash totals last year was because its post office operatives did not want to alert criminals to the amount of money they had on the premises. Branches are vulnerable to theft for the same reason they are wide open to money laundering. They are often just ordinary shops offering post-office services over the counter, and they lack the specialised equipment that would allow them to track who is on the premises, or to keep their employees safe.
Back when Post Office Ltd was still publishing its monthly cash figures, it would accompany them with upbeat quotes about how much it was helping small businesses by providing banking services. While much of the increase is certainly being driven by the closure of bank branches, a senior police officer would regularly forward the figures to me, accompanied with a single emoji: 👀.
Concerns about being seen to further victimise post office operatives has discouraged police officers from going on the record about the scale of the problem that they’re seeing. “I’m sure you appreciate that anything quotable is going to have to be suitably vanilla,” another senior officer told me. “It would need to be, you know, ‘we work in partnership’, ‘there are many perspectives’-type stuff.”
The sensitivity is understandable, but it comes with dangers. By making it possible for organised criminals – drug dealers, human traffickers, thieves, fraudsters and others – to launder their earnings, and thus to keep their profits, the post office risks creating an entirely different scandal.
The trial of Giuseppe Sangiovanni and seven of his alleged co-conspirators was due to start in May 2025 at Bristol crown court, and to run for several days. Sangiovanni was accused of running a scheme that laundered £2.2m via post office branches in Bristol and Gloucestershire over a few months of 2021. His alleged co-conspirators were accused of letting him move money through their bank accounts in return for small payments.
On the first morning of the trial, however, Sangiovanni changed his plea to guilty and left the courtroom to await a fresh hearing, leaving his co-defendants behind. It quickly became clear that they were not criminal masterminds. I had only just arrived in Bristol and knew only the bare outlines of the case, but even I could tell their chances of escaping conviction were now close to nonexistent. If the prosecutors had all the transaction details, and the ringleader was admitting the charges, then the owners of the bank accounts through which the money had passed would find it all but impossible to convince a jury that nothing untoward had occurred.
Technically, a trial was still scheduled, but it was so obviously not going to happen that the jury never even entered the courtroom. The two prosecution lawyers, far from wargaming the new reality, were using the break to discuss holiday destinations for their unexpected spell of spare time. The only people present who appeared not to realise the consequences of Sangiovanni’s decision were his co-defendants, who continued to sit in the dock like baby birds in smart casual, with only the haziest of ideas what was going on.
The judge tried to help, encouraging them to discuss things with their lawyers. They whispered among themselves, until one at a time – over the course of many hours, and after many hearings were convened, suspended and convened again – they changed their pleas to guilty too. (They were not masterminds, as I say, and mostly received suspended sentences.)
“They’re just run-of-the-mill local criminals. A couple of them weren’t really criminals at all. One that we didn’t charge was a single mum and, to a degree, was exploited,” said Detective Inspector Peter Highway of the south west regional organised crime unit. It was only while being interviewed by police that one defendant discovered that Sangiovanni had laundered more than £1m through his bank account. “He was a bit surprised by that number,” said Highway, “because he hadn’t done the deposits himself.”
Money laundering was criminalised in the UK in 1988 as part of a global effort to close loopholes in the financial system that were allowing criminals to keep their profits. Previously, it had been easy for criminals to walk into a bank and pay in cash, no questions asked, but the new laws obliged bankers to report suspicious transactions to law enforcement agencies. The theory was that, with bankers sending in a steady stream of suspicious activity reports, police officers would be able to see money being laundered in real time, freeze it and arrest its owners.
The world has moved on since then and the most sophisticated crime, such as fraud, involves electronic money stolen from people’s bank accounts and moved in a bewildering variety of ways, involving shell companies, cryptocurrencies, secrecy jurisdictions and more. This requires equally advanced countermeasures from banks, which use AI-powered tools to spot the signs of criminal behaviour.
At the street level, however, not much has changed: criminals still use cash, and the National Crime Agency estimates that they launder about £12bn worth of banknotes in the UK each year, largely by presenting the money as the fruits of legitimate businesses. This is where branches of the post office come in.
From the criminals’ point of view, post offices are quick and easy places to launder dodgy money. “There’s no requirement for ID verification, there’s no requirement for any kind of enhanced screening, there’s no centralised CCTV,” said the second senior police officer. We put a higher bar on buying alcohol than we do on money laundering via the post office.
This is why Gheewala’s mules were able to go into a branch with a pocket full of bank cards, and pay bundles of cash into multiple accounts, one after another. “You definitely don’t want, in a post office that has already got queues out the door, to have a complicated financial transaction going on. So everything that the post office does for banking is done with simplicity in mind,” said the former Post Office employee.
The trouble then is, as happened in Leicester, that criminals move money onwards as soon as it arrives in a bank account. Any reports that post office employees do make about the transaction will come too late for the bank to be able to freeze it. This defangs the UK’s entire anti-money-laundering strategy, which has always relied on being able to block suspicious transactions while officers investigate them.
The criminal possibilities opened up by Post Office Ltd’s foray into banking were quickly obvious. In July 2020, the Post Office’s compliance committee noted £7m of questionable deposits had gone into 45 branches. In November that year, it discussed how £5-7m a week was being deposited at just two branches in east London, and said it was discussing with the banks what action to take.
Sangiovanni and his co-defendants fell foul of this kind of scrutiny, after bank compliance officers spotted what amounted to millions of pounds of suspicious cash transactions at 27 post offices around Gloucestershire, and alerted the police who brought in first the mules, then Sangiovanni, for questioning. “He gave an account that he would go to a car park at Asda, and someone would give him a carrier bag full of cash, and he would then take it away, and then send them some crypto,” said Highway. “He didn’t feel that was suspicious. We did.”
By the time officers from the south west organised crime unit moved in, however, the money was long gone. So, although they caught Sangiovanni, the criminals whose cash he was laundering got to enjoy the freshly laundered money. “Millions of pounds into the laundering, that’s a bit late in the day,” said Highway.
It looks obvious how to close this gap in our defences against dirty cash. If the Post Office is going to act like a bank, it should collect the same kind of information as a bank, make the same kind of reports as a bank, and freeze transactions in the same way that banks do. In 2023, the regulators at the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) took a small step in this direction, by imposing limits on how much cash could be deposited at the post office at any one time. It was a logical step to take, but it ran into immediate controversy.
The fact that two-thirds of bank branches have closed in the UK in the past decade has left businesses and individuals who still rely on cash heavily dependent on post-office branches to pay in their takings. Post Office Ltd used this fact to push back against the FCA’s deposit limits by saying they were penalising hard-pressed businesses that were just trying to stay afloat. “They are hurting legitimate customers and businesses who need support,” said Ross Borkett, Post Office Ltd’s then-head of banking, after the FCA’s changes were announced. Cash-intensive businesses, via the British Independent Retailers Association and the Independent Retail Consortium, mobilised a lobbying operation, writing to their MPs, who in turn held debates in parliament to highlight how few bank branches were left in their constituencies.
As a result, ministers promised to ensure that businesses and individuals still reliant on banknotes and coins would always be able to use them. In other words, the FCA’s cash limit is likely to be the last intervention to make payments at post offices harder.
At a time when an increasingly large proportion of the population can’t access a physical bank branch, the 11,500 post-office branches in the UK will become ever-more central to a strategy of ensuring everyone can still use banknotes. Moving, securing and accepting cash is expensive though, which is one reason why the banks don’t much want to do it any more. Post offices don’t charge their customers for making deposits, however, so who is going to pay for it?
The answer to that question is tied up in the legacy of the Horizon scandal. Post Office Ltd was already in significant financial difficulties before it began having to pay compensation to the hundreds of post office operatives that it had unfairly prosecuted. It has now had to distribute more than £1bn, pushing it into a deep annual loss.
That is already a significant challenge for its long-term viability, but it is only half of the problem it faces. Post-office branches operate as independent businesses, but the amount of money operatives earned from providing post office services fell by almost 5% in the decade to 2023, in part thanks to fewer people sending letters. Meanwhile, post office operatives’ expenses have increased. So Post Office Ltd not only needs to find the money to pay compensation to the post office operatives it has wronged, but it must also simultaneously find a sustainable business model if it wants people to be post office operatives at all. And that is where banking comes in.
Banks pay Post Office Ltd for providing services on their behalf, which helped it to post revenues of £309m from “banking and ATMs” in its 2024-5 accounts. That was more than a third of its revenues for that year, and only slightly less than it earned from handling the mail. In fact, Post Office Ltd may already be making more money from deposits and withdrawals than it does from its traditional business. As the former insider joked: “We should start calling it the Bank Office.”
This isn’t just important for Post Office Ltd, but also for individual post office operatives, who earn a fee for every cash deposit they accept. “The post office operatives will be remunerated on the transactions that they have through their branch, so they will get a transaction fee,” Ben Woollard, the new head of banking at Post Office Ltd, told me. “As with any product, the more a post office operative or any business will deliver, then they will earn more income out of that.”
Woollard argues that post-office branches are no different from any other business in being vulnerable to money laundering. He pointed out to me that anyone offering banking services receives annual training in how to recognise and tackle money laundering, and that the head office sends out alerts to branches in areas that appear to have a large number of suspicious transactions.
But although any business that handles cash could be exploited by criminals, it is also true that few businesses handle banknotes in the volumes that routinely pass through post-office branches, making them more vulnerable to abuse than most. Post office operatives are also running a system that we know is already wide open to dirty money, and are rewarded proportionally to the raw total of money they put through it, so the temptation to look the other way or even to provide financial services to criminals must be ever-present.
We have no idea how many insiders have given in to this temptation, and it looks likely that we will remain in the dark. The disastrous legacy of the Horizon scandal means there has been little appetite to investigate. With such a deeply flawed system, the best that police officers can hope for is to prosecute the more egregious offenders.
So despite the success of Operation Kilo, Leicestershire police’s Detective Constable Catherine Richards wasn’t exactly optimistic that Gheewala’s conviction would change anything: “Crime is continuing,” she told me. “Money needs to be laundered. And, yeah, somebody else fills those boots, don’t they?”

items.body:
Target, the US retail corporation, said it pulled a controversial Halloween costume off its shelves after criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature.
The ad image for the costume, sold as the “Kids’ Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume,” depicted a Black child in a bright orange and black top with solid black gloves and a mask with a wide, toothy smile. Both the child’s pose and the costume’s gloves and mask were likened to caricatures of Black people used in minstrel shows.
“As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry,” Target said in its apology statement. “The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale. We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won’t happen again.”
The costume controversy is just the latest in a series for the Minneapolis-based retailer.
Last year, activists called for a boycott of the company, after its decision to walk-back DEI initiatives. And last week, the American Federation of Teachers, a teachers’ union, called on Target’s CEO, Michael Fiddelke, to call for an end to Operation Metro Surge, Trump’s National Guard push in Minneapolis earlier this year.
Target’s stock price decreased from $137.40 on 24 January, the day the company cut its DEI programs, to $104.70 on 15 March. The company is starting to experience a financial comeback after the initial boycott, but could face other challenges.
