items.body:
When I tell people I spent a chunk of my early 20s working at a hipster clothing retailer infamous for salacious ads and sexual assault allegations, I’m usually met with scandalised interest. I imagine what they imagine: a harshly lit harem of flesh and vice, where young women were offered up on an altar of mid-priced T-shirts.
We had our moments. An occasional visiting corporate lackey would inevitably grind up against one of us while checking a window display. A weekly caller would gasp and choke while asking if we sold women’s underwear. A co-worker inquired whether I’d be interested in going on dates with rich, interesting men for money. It was impossible to ignore the reputation of our store. But it was the 2010s, a strangely liminal time of sexual and social awakening. When we could roll our eyes at the problematic gender politics of our advertisements while never considering wearing a bra to work.
But the truth is, despite the global reputation, our little store in Melbourne was one of the most positive workplaces of my life.
The store was divided into two tribes: shop assistants – mostly doe-eyed art girls – and backstock workers – mostly charming burnout skaters. While the shop assistants got the most attention and lustful public glares, the weed-scented heart of the store was the backstock room.
I was a rare breed: a shop assistant who transitioned to a backstock role, mostly because I couldn’t use a cash register properly.
Despite technically being a demotion, the move made me the envy of the shop assistants. In backstock we’d listen to music while folding T-shirts and debating Simpsons lore like greasy-haired scholars.
After hours we drove around listening to music, slept in each other’s beds, held pizza parties, dated friends of friends, occasionally kissed and sometimes fell in love.
Memories of this time seem to exist in an endless summer, where it was always warm twilight at closing time. Even when winter rain flooded through the roof and we mopped up dirty puddles with damaged clearance stock. It felt less like a sexy party and more like wholesome summer camp.
Central to this group was our boss, who was barely 30 but held the role of paternal authority. He guided our rambling crew of bleary-eyed adult children through the basic requirements of our jobs.
He ran a tight ship. We might have smelled like cheap wine but we worked hard, dutifully memorising our SKU codes and ensuring the dickheads of Melbourne were kept in a steady supply of lamé leggings.
After about two years of this heavenly haze, he pulled me aside. Ensconced in piles of chunky acrylic knits, he broke the news: “You have to quit.”
I was shocked. Yes, I was famously bad at my job. But his directive wasn’t based on my shirt-folding incompetence.
The problem was I loved the job so much I’d never leave.
He knew I wanted to be a writer. Occasionally I’d pick up a passing freelance gig or have a submission accepted. But in the time I’d been working happily at the store, my career had made little progress.
With this context, he made something clear that I’d been too afraid to admit to myself: this fantasy life was stopping me from beginning my real one.
He pointed out that instead of being satisfied, I was satiated. I had just enough fun to keep me ticking along day after day. This was, he stressed, exactly the kind of job that could trap you.
It was a tough lesson, and one I didn’t receive immediately. But slinking away, I reflected on how little I’d actually written. How many days were full of work I liked but hardly lived for.
Within a month, I’d applied for an internship that would lead to the job that would shape the rest of my 20s and kickstart my life as a professional writer. It often made me stressed, angry and exhausted, but it also expanded my abilities and sense of self.
Fifteen years and many jobs and careers later, I still return to that advice. It’s not that I don’t want to feel comfortable and happy. Rather, I’m aware of the sticky allure of “good enough”. A job, relationship, situation that isn’t actively bad, but isn’t what I truly want or deserve.
Although, even now, nothing relaxes me like folding a T-shirt.

items.title: Pubs and hotels could see business rates reformed after review
items.summary: The review of how rates are calculated in England and Wales could lead to reform of the system.
items.body:
Pubs and hotels could see business rates reformed after review
- Published
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.
The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.
Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.
Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.
According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.
Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.
James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".
Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."
The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade (FMT) - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.
Jonathan Lawson, the chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs across the south and south west of England, told the BBC's Today programme that the use of FMT meant pubs were effectively being "punished for success", while large online retailers that operate out of warehouses were not subject to revenue-based rates calculations.
Their rates, he said, "are calculated based on what is deemed to be the market rent for that area, and takes very little on board in terms of revenue driven through that site".
"You can have a very large site paying a relatively low level of business rates versus a relatively small pub... paying a very high level of business rates."
Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.
Northern Ireland and Scotland set their own valuations, while Wales presently chooses to align its methodology with England. As the same approach is used across England and Wales, the review will be looking for responses from both nations.
Schurder's appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".
However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.
Jonny Haseldine from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also said the review of valuations should be wider.
"The full reform of business rates, promised by the government at the last election, is urgently needed. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach," he said.
While the BCC said hospitality was the sector most worried about rates, Haseldine warned firms in every sector were struggling with the "complex and outdated" system.
Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".
"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".
Last year, under the previous chancellor Rachel Reeves, the government had said it would scale back business rate discounts that had been in force since the Covid pandemic and announced that there would be no discount at all from April this year.
That, combined with big upward adjustments to rateable values of pub premises, left landlords with the prospect of much higher bills.
Following criticism from the hospitality industry, the government cut business rates for pubs and music venues by 15% earlier in 2026.
The 20% discount in England announced in July will apply on top of the existing support.

items.body:
Shein, which built a fast-fashion empire on what seemed like impossibly low prices, has been forced to lower its own valuation in a cut-price stock market float, after falling into the red earlier this year.
The online retailer will list on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September at a valuation of close to $27bn (£19.8bn), significantly down from a near-$100bn private market peak four years ago.
It is one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings (IPO) of recent years, after plans to list in New York were blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns. Shein then considered a £50bn float in London, but faced similar questions about its supply chain from campaigners, MPs and investors.
The company moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, a move analysts have said was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.
In early 2025 it refused to reassure British MPs that its products do not include cotton produced in the Xinjiang region of China, which has been linked to forced Uyghur labour.
Founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, the company runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world.
But more recently it has faced questions over slowing growth and rising costs. It swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the US removed an import duty exemption on small packages, hitting its sales in the country.
The company said the Iran war had caused delays to deliveries in some of its leading markets, while there was also less demand for its products because of the economic fallout from the conflict.
Shein said on Monday it would offer nearly 280m shares for between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50 each. That would raise roughly £1.3bn for the company at the top end of the range, and give it a market valuation of just under £20bn. The final offer price will be set on the day before it starts trading on 1 September.
The company’s European customer base rose to 156 million average monthly users by the end of last year, making it one of the continent’s biggest e-commerce platforms alongside Amazon.
Shein partly benefits from sending goods directly to shoppers, including to the UK and US, from China so they attract fewer taxes. The tactic has prompted calls for a change in tax rules.
In November, the group opened its first-ever physical outlet, a dedicated space in the BHV department store in Paris. Hundreds of customers lined up on its opening day, and dozens more people gathered to protest, requiring a heavy police presence.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “Shein may still be one of the biggest names on the fast-fashion catwalk, but the IPO is going to be a harder sell, with plenty of investors questioning whether its low-cost formula still has the star power to deliver the growth they’re looking for.’’

items.title: ‘Penchant for bling’: can Sports Direct’s Mike Ashley take a bigger slice of luxury retail?
items.summary: Frasers billionaire bought Harvey Nichols and increased Hugo Boss stake despite tough times for high-end stores What billionaire doesn’t love to splash the cash on a luxury item? Some may buy watches or yachts, but Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has been snapping up entire brands. Harvey Nichols is the latest bauble to drop into his shopping basket after his company bought the Knightsbridge department store out of administration earlier this month. It sits beside a large slice of Hugo Boss, a chunk of Mulberry, a snippet of Burberry, the remains of Agent Provocateur and the entire Flannels and House of Fraser chains. Continue reading...
items.body:
What billionaire doesn’t love to splash the cash on a luxury item? Some may buy watches or yachts, but Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has been snapping up entire brands.
Harvey Nichols is the latest bauble to drop into his shopping basket after his company bought the Knightsbridge department store out of administration earlier this month. It sits beside a large slice of Hugo Boss, a chunk of Mulberry, a snippet of Burberry, the remains of Agent Provocateur and the entire Flannels and House of Fraser chains.
After a rough few years for the sellers of luxury goods – as the cost of living crisis has crunched the spare cash aspirational consumers might have had available for the occasional treat, and Asian and Middle Eastern shoppers have become less inclined to travel to Europe – Ashley’s buying spree might seem out of sync.
However, the string of acquisitions closely match the entrepreneur’s established modus operandi – picking up bargains during tough times and finding the value where he can.
Sports Direct, now part of Ashley’s Frasers Group, built its business by snapping up struggling independent sporting goods chains and bumped up its profits by getting the UK rights to ailing sportswear brands – from Head to Slazenger – and using them to decorate its own products.
Since first buying a stake in Flannels in 2012, then a menswear store in Knutsford, Cheshire, Ashley has been slowly building a luxury portfolio.
The strategy has had its ups and downs. Flannels has expanded to about 75 stores and now sells brands from Gucci to Stone Island to Maison Margiela. This week, Ashley celebrated lifting his stake in the German label Hugo Boss to 48%, just short of taking full control, despite opposition from the company’s board.
The Harvey Nichols deal is a classic tactic to gain access to intransigent brands, adding lustre to the portfolio that could make some designer marques previously shy of engaging with the king of discount trainers sit up.
Ashley is likely to take a pragmatic approach to the wider Harvey Nichols estate, having said he intends to convert at least some of the five UK outposts outside London to the Flannels brand.
However, labels pondering whether to continue supplying the department store chain might do well to consider the events at the luxury online fashion seller Matchesfashion. Frasers bought the business for £52m at the end of 2023, only to place it into administration months later, leaving millions of pounds owed to designer brands.
House of Fraser is another cautionary tale. On buying the House of Fraser chain of 60 department stores out of administration almost exactly eight years ago, he set a mission to become “the Harrods of the high street”. Today there are just five stores left trading under that name.
There are another 15 stores badged as just Frasers, some of which are converted department stores while others are somewhat smaller sites. The Frasers name is also being used on a Luton shopping mall in the group’s property portfolio, which contains a House of Fraser discount outlet.
Such a confusing brand story is unlikely to entice large international labels to engage. Even the Flannels chain, Frasers said in its latest annual results published in July, was “now near complete”, indicating it did not intend to add many more stores.
Sales at the group’s “premium lifestyle” division, which includes House of Fraser and Jack Wills, fell almost 7%, while profits fell by almost £10m to £147.6m. Frasers said this included a rise in sales at Flannels, but gave no figures, so it was unclear if that was driven by adding new stores.
Luxury fashion acquisitions by Frasers do not appear to have flourished. Jack Wills, once widely sported by partying public schoolers on their holidays in Cornwall, now has just five independent outlets, down from about 100 when Frasers bought it in 2019.
Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital, said that if one examined the group’s spending on upmarket brands then “from a financial perspective it has not been a roaring success.
“The premium end of Frasers has been a burden for the wider group. The mothership is Sports Direct and that’s what is funding the wider diversification strategy.”
He suggested the strategy was more driven by Ashley’s personal aspiration to be taken seriously by these big names. “He has developed a penchant for bling in his 60s,” Black said. Whether “buying assets at the bottom” will lead to a benefit if and when the market improves works out “only time will tell”, he added.
Luxury market experts are also sceptical. One told the Guardian he would not have chosen to buy Harvey Nichols as its brand had become degraded and customers had gone elsewhere.
He suggested the building’s freeholders – the Cadogan Estate – had long discussed a plan to turn Harvey Nichols into a hotel or apartments and this might be the ultimate future of much of the Knightsbridge site.
Another industry insider said that, while rivals Selfridges and Harrods had been revitalised, Harvey Nichols “just feels like its lost its way”.
The old hand suggested Ashley’s scattergun expansion may yet lead him astray, pointing to the failed retail empires of Sears and Arcadia, and Marks & Spencer’s ill-fated efforts to expand overseas with Brooks Brothers. He suggested that running luxury brands such as Hugo Boss and Harvey Nichols might be a “bit of an overreach. It’s very different to a volume play.”
He said it was clear Frasers had a weaker business than Next, where chief executive Simon Wolfson’s buying spree is strictly limited to strong brands with effective management teams that need help to succeed online using Next’s expertise and infrastructure.
“The world of retail is littered with big organisations with an existing business that liked to acquire other brands and it doesn’t manage to succeed or end well,” the insider said. However, he added of Ashley: “I wouldn’t bet against him.”
The businessman has a long history as a gambler, famously producing a wad of £50 notes from his pocket when taking journalists through security screening on a visit to the company’s Shirebrook warehouse in Derbyshire.
He is not averse to risk but most of his business deals are underpinned by the value of stock and or property, which can be traded to raise cash if other tactics fail. The future for Harvey Nichols and its new luxury brand stablemates might not be pretty, but Ashley is likely to make money however it turns out.
Frasers Group declined to comment.

items.title: ‘It brings me joy’: how young people are making CDs cool again
items.summary: Compact discs are back, with searches for players up 96% at John Lewis and popular models sold out online With more than 800 million people subscribing to a music streaming service, wireless speakers have become a familiar sight in homes. But expect to get reacquainted with a different object to play music soon: the CD player, once consigned to obsolescence, is back. John Lewis report that searches for CD players are up 96% since July, possibly owing to students heading to university and buying the systems for their rooms. The £79 Crosley Voyager , and the £129 Pure Classic C-D6 are both sold out online, with the Voyager scheduled to return in October. Portable CD players are also popular. Continue reading...
items.body:
With more than 800 million people subscribing to a music streaming service, wireless speakers have become a familiar sight in homes. But expect to get reacquainted with a different object to play music soon: the CD player, once consigned to obsolescence, is back.
John Lewis report that searches for CD players are up 96% since July, possibly owing to students heading to university and buying the systems for their rooms. The £79 Crosley Voyager, and the £129 Pure Classic C-D6 are both sold out online, with the Voyager scheduled to return in October. Portable CD players are also popular.
This tallies, of course, with sales of CDs themselves. A report this year found that the growth of CD sales is up 16%, compared with vinyl’s 2.4%. HMV reports that sales of CDs are up 10% year on year – thanks to artists often providing unique content on the format. “K-pop has been a massive driver, with BTS the most obvious example of artists that have led the resurgence,” says the managing director, Phil Halliday. “But it goes much wider than that. We’re seeing very strong CD demand around artists like Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Olivia Dean.”
The fact that a vinyl record is about £35, compared with £12 for a CD, is no doubt a factor.
Tom Morgan-Freelander, the deputy editor of the technology magazine Stuff, has noticed the change over the past two years. He puts it down to consumers wanting to move away from using their phone, a better audio quality, and limited disposable income. “It’s: ‘I don’t want to spend money on a turntable and the speakers that go with it. I want to spend £150 on an all-in-one system that comes with the CD player,’” he says.
In the CD aisle of an HMV in London on a weekday morning, people in their teens and twenties are browsing. Fourteen-year-old Milo Georgeaux-Healy has chosen two Dua Lipa albums as well as Brat by Charli xcx to play on an “old boombox”. “I like them because they’re cheaper,” she says. “They’re a lot more compact [than vinyl], and I find that they have better quality than your phone.” Adel Alsehi, 27, is visiting from Riyadh. He has selected a Madonna greatest hits, a Kacey Musgraves album and Private Dancer by Tina Turner. “It gives me a different feeling,” he says of CDs. “I feel like I’m listening to an artist’s work. It brings me joy.”
Richard Farnell runs Vinyl Exchange in Manchester, where they also sell CDs. He says the people buying CDs are now younger, and cost is a big part of this. “The record labels started to up the price of vinyl and it became largely unaffordable for this demographic,” he says. “A copy of Oasis’s Definitely Maybe on original UK “Damont” pressing can sell for between £150 and £250, depending upon condition. The standard vinyl reissue will be around £25-£30, but in our shop the CD version will only be £4.”
The CD revival is part of a wider fashion for retro tech. As well as the vinyl resurgence and cassettes becoming popular items to buy, there’s the vogue for wearing wired earphones over AirPods. “The vinyl revival re-established our appetite for analogue, and now we’re seeing that broader love for physical music drive a genuine surge in CD players,” confirms Katrina Mills, the category buying lead for audio and imaging at John Lewis.
Part of this is about optics. “Someone walking around with a portable CD player and wired headphones is signalling their sense of taste and cultural capital,” says brand strategist Alexi Gunner. He has labelled this trend “performative audiophilia”.
Gunner argues that the return to the physical for music is a kind of rebellion. “The status quo is streaming platforms and wireless audio on identical iPhones,” he says. “All this has taken away the haptic, sensorial quality of listening to music.”
J’Nae Phillips, who writes about Gen Z trends on her Substack Fashion Tingz, agrees. “When music is effectively infinite and frictionless, something is appealing about having to choose an album, put a disc in and listen to it from beginning to end,” she says, and echoes Gunner’s point: “There’s a certain cultural cachet in showing that you’re interested in music as an object and an experience, rather than simply consuming whatever happens to be recommended by an algorithm.”
Arguably, the CD is the final revival available to young people – it’s the last format for music before the MP3 arrived in the early 2000s. However, Gunner suggests there may be a different object waiting in the wings: the USB stick. Fred Again named his 2025 tour after the portable drive. “It’s the most common format that a DJ will carry their music to a gig on,” explains Gunner. “In the frame of performative audiophilia, you’re showing that you’re not just listening to music, you are possibly a DJ, you are a tastemaker … it’s something that will become more popular.”

items.title: Quarter of branded baby foods in UK still have too much sugar, analysis finds
items.summary: Exclusive: Of 224 branded infant foods and snacks, more than half are in breach of guidelines brought in a year ago Almost a quarter of popular branded baby foods sold in UK supermarkets still contain excessive amounts of sugar, analysis suggests, a year after the government introduced voluntary industry guidelines . In August 2025 the government gave baby food manufacturers 18 months to reduce the sugar and salt content of their products, stop marketing snacks to infants under 12 months, and address misleading and inaccurate labelling that makes some infant foods appear healthier than they actually are. Continue reading...
items.body:
Almost a quarter of popular branded baby foods sold in UK supermarkets still contain excessive amounts of sugar, analysis suggests, a year after the government introduced voluntary industry guidelines.
In August 2025 the government gave baby food manufacturers 18 months to reduce the sugar and salt content of their products, stop marketing snacks to infants under 12 months, and address misleading and inaccurate labelling that makes some infant foods appear healthier than they actually are.
An analysis of 224 branded infant foods and snacks has found that, a year on, more than half (58%) breached at least one of the nine guidelines and that a quarter of all products breached two or more.
Nora Cavani, the chief executive and co-founder of Alba Health, a gut health company that conducted the analysis, said: “Parents are not failing their children – they are being misled. Products that contain more sugar than a child should consume in a day are sold under the banner of health and nature. A year on from the guidelines’ introduction, the data shows voluntary standards haven’t worked.”
The foods studied included purees, breakfast, main meals, desserts, snacks and finger foods made by nine of the UK’s leading brands: Ella’s Kitchen, Heinz, Organix, HiPP, Kiddylicious, Little Freddie, Piccolo, Aptamil and Cow & Gate.
Of these, 51 (23%) contained too much sugar, including 52% of Kiddylicious’s products, 28% of Piccolo’s, 27% of Heinz’s, and 24% of Little Freddie products. In the case of five products, more than 80% of the total calories were from sugar, including Organix raisins, which contained 66g of sugar per 100g (86.6% kcal from sugars) and Kiddylicious apple fruit wriggles, which contained 70g of sugar per 100g (85.6% sugars).
The NHS recommends that babies under one consume less than 1g of salt a day, but the analysis found about 6% of foods – 14 products – breached those limits, with Heinz spaghetti bolognese pouches containing 0.27g of salt, more than a quarter of an infant’s entire daily allowance in one meal. In all, 19% of Kiddylicious’s products, 18% of HiPP’s, 13% of Heinz’s and 6% of Cow & Gate’s breached the Office for Health Improvement and Disparity (OHID) salt and sodium guidelines.
Labelling and marketing breaches were found in 28% of products, including 31 snacks marketed at children as young as six months old, while labels on others made misleading health claims.
Experts said the data showed that the voluntary approach had failed. Prof Steve Turner, the president of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, said: “Paediatricians have long raised concerns about the high levels of salt and sugar in some infant and baby foods, and the impact this can have on children’s long-term health, including obesity and poor oral health.
“Ensuring baby food is nutritious, and does not encourage children to develop a preference for sugary foods later in life, is essential. We are clear that only mandatory nutritional standards and regulation of these products will provide the protection babies and children need.”
Sonia Pombo, the head of research and impact at Action on Salt and Sugar, said it was striking that there were problems among brands that positioned themselves as organic or healthy. “Parents should be able to trust that the name and imagery on the front of a pack accurately reflect what is inside, yet when a product is promoted using an appealing fruit or vegetable despite not being the main ingredient, it risks misleading parents,” she said.
“With only six months until the February 2027 compliance deadline, voluntary action is clearly not delivering quickly enough. If the government is serious about protecting babies and young children, these guidelines should be made mandatory and properly enforced.”
A spokesperson for the British Specialist Nutrition Association, which represents the infant food industry, said: “BSNA members welcomed the government’s guidance and have been fully engaged with OHID throughout its development. Significant progress has already been made, including reducing sugar and increasing vegetable content. Ultimately reformulation takes time, and the government recognised this when setting a deadline of February 2027 for compliance.
“Parents can feel confident that members are on track to meet the guidance, offering convenient, nutritious choices that support the realities of modern family life.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “We want every child to have the best possible start in life, and that includes making sure the food available to babies and young children is as healthy as possible. We have already taken action, publishing targets to reduce sugar and salt and introducing guidelines to improve labelling in baby food and drink, with industry given until February 2027 to make these changes.
“We will continue to work with industry to make sure parents can make healthy choices for their children.”

items.summary: Volume of goods sold in stores and online dropped 0.5% in July, ONS says Business live – latest updates Retail sales across Great Britain weakened last month despite the men’s football World Cup and record temperatures boosting the demand for food and drink. items.body:
Retail sales across Great Britain weakened last month despite the men’s football World Cup and record temperatures boosting the demand for food and drink.
The Office for National Statistics said the volume of goods sold in stores and online fell 0.5% in July. That is down from 0.7% rise in June – revised down from initial estimates of 1% – and a 1.3% rise in May.
Non-food stores took the biggest tumble, falling 1.3%, on the back of a drop in clothes shopping, after retailers brought forward cut-price sales into June while heatwaves in July resulted in more people staying home than hitting the high street.
Sandra Prince, the head of consumer at Lloyds, said: “Hotter days could have shifted footfall and spending online or towards retail parks. For retailers, as the summer peak slows down, attention is now turning to the opportunities the autumn could bring to keep consumers engaged.”
Demand for furniture also took a dive, with fewer households looking to change decor during the extreme heat, while department stores suffered because of a drop in available stock. Some retailers had warned of lengthier delivery times during recent heatwaves.
Food and drink sales were a rare bright spot, however, as hot and sunny weather and excitement around World Cup games boosted demand.
However, the gains could have been higher had it not been for pubs and sports bars – which count as hospitality rather than retail in official statistics – luring punters to their screens to watch big matches.
The British Beer & Pub Association said last month that late opening hours and England’s progress to the semi-finals gave a big boost to the industry, with pubs pouring an extra 30m pints than normal over the course of the tournament. That produced an extra £150m in added sales for its members.
Jacqui Baker, a partner and the head of retail at the consultancy RSM UK, said: “Retail was not a World Cup winner, with many opting to cheer on England from the pub and prioritising their summer getaway, boosting hospitality and travel rather than retail sales.
“Consumers splashed out on fans and food for barbeques due to the heatwave, with many avoiding soaring temperatures on the high street.”

items.body:
Good morning. I could mark the phases of my life through my charity shop purchases: the tweedy jackets of my student days, the nearly new hiking boots (a tenner!) I bought out of necessity when I first arrived back in Scotland, the battered guitar now re-strung for my son to practise Nirvana’s About a Girl.
Since they became a fixture of high streets after the second world war, charity shops have rolled with the punches of wider retail trends. In the 80s, they were showered with tax breaks to take up vacant space as supermarkets put grocers and butchers out of business. At the end of the noughties, after the global financial crash, retail legend Mary Portas promoted charity shops as a vehicle for reviving the high street. And as awareness grows of the planetary penalty of throwaway textiles, next month heralds Second Hand September, Oxfam’s annual campaign to highlight fashion’s environmental damage.
But recent headlines about shop closures – including the potential closure of 100 Oxfam outlets – and sustained pressures from the boom in secondhand selling online suggest a deeper crisis in the sector. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Vicki Burnett, a charity retail expert who has volunteered in charity shops since the age of 15, about why community is key to the sector’s continued success. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK news | Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media.
-

In depth: ‘With the glut of fast fashion quality donations have reduced’
When “Everybody’s Thrift Shop”, one of Britain’s earliest recorded charity shops, was opened at 79a Nicholson Street, Edinburgh, in 1937, the Scotsman reported queues outside and police on hand to manage restive shoppers.
“One woman went off triumphant with a handsome suit once worn, it was whispered, by a professor. Another secured a real bargain: 10 shirts for half-a-crown.”
The second world war spurred the popularity of temporary fundraising shops, and the escalating humanitarian crisis led to the formation of Oxfam, which opened its first permanent outlet on Broad Street, Oxford, in 1947.
By the 1960s many other charities had done the same, as the demise of wartime “make do and mend” saw the secondhand clothing market expand, and over subsequent decades the sector was increasingly professionalised, with specialist shops opening for music and books.
There are now 10,000 charity shops across the UK, staffed by about 223,000 volunteers and 24,900 paid employees, and raising over £300m profit in 2024/25. But their future is not secure.
What are the pressures on charity retail?
Oxfam is considering closing up to 100 of its 500-plus UK retail outlets, the Guardian reported earlier this week.
In June, the British Heart Foundation announced plans to close about 150 stores over the next two financial years “to ensure our retail network remains commercially sustainable,” and last October, Cancer Research confirmed it would be shutting 90 shops across the UK.
Costs have increased across retail in recent years. While charities don’t have to pay business rates, they are still hit by increases in national insurance and wage bills. The drop in town centre footfall, accelerated by Covid, is well documented. And indeed the decline of the British high street, with its dispiriting template of boarded up premises, betting shops and vape outlets, has become a political shorthand for a far wider malaise.
An Oxfam insider told the Guardian that shops were facing a fall in donations, as well as competition from online sellers of secondhand goods such as Vinted, now the fourth largest clothing retailers in the country, eBay and Depop.
This proliferation of alternative places to buy pre-loved fashion offers ease, often at a more competitive price point.
With only a cameraphone and decent wifi needed to join the market, a public seeking to monetise every last unwanted item amid the ongoing cost of living crisis has become less willing to donate, particularly more profitable items.
Charity shops are also facing a slump in recycling income. The price of “rag” – poor quality, unsellable clothing that is sold on in bulk for recycling to use as shredded fibres for mattress or insulation, for example – has dived in recent years, and a substantial source of profit has evaporated.
How is charity retail evolving?
Beyond these headline closures, those working within the sector suggest a more layered analysis. The Charity Retail Association reports an increase in overall sales space among its members – but a significant trend towards closing smaller shops in favour of larger stores, especially among bigger charities.
With the glut of fast fashion, all across the sector agree that quality donations have reduced – but there has been no reduction in quantity.
In fact, the advent of resellers – people who are coming to the shops to buy stock to resell themselves online at profit – is now providing charity shops with significant income and creating a virtuous circle: as outlets like Vinted normalise the secondhand clothing market, it encourages people to explore charity shops themselves.
Communities offline and online
The charity retail sector has faced tough times before, says Vicki Burnett, a senior consultant for the Charity Retail Consultancy, who advises clients of different sizes on how to go with the grain of evolving tech and remain rooted in local communities.
All charities need to keep their retail entities under constant review, Burnett tells me, but assessing a shop’s contribution goes well beyond the financial, as communities themselves recognised during the pandemic.
“People had really missed their charity shops. They don’t just bring in cash,” she says.
When she moved from Leeds to Argyll, Burnett started volunteering in her local Oxfam “as a way to get myself into my community, to understand a bit more about it”. A charity shop is a place where youngsters struggling with fragile mental health and a brutal jobs market – who Hettie wrote about yesterday – can gain CV skills alongside some gentle interaction. Many charities now deliver an element of their service through their shops, whether that’s healthcare education or details of animals available for rehoming nearby, something that’s easier to do in the larger format “one-stop” stores that are now emerging.
Charity retailers have been selling online for many years, Burnett reminds me. Ebay, for example, has mentored many charities through online selling and there’s the hope that Vinted and other commercial resellers will follow suit.
What is new is the volume of resellers and content creators. There are now so many working semi-professionally that the Charity Retail Association is about to launch an expanded directory of hundreds of charity shop influencers based around the country ready to collaborate with retailers. One of them, Emily London, offers charity shops tours and second hand personal styling alongside her own online resale shop.
“Influencers are a fantastic resource for charities and great advocates for pre-loved clothing,” says Burnett (If you’re looking for advice, then vintage maven and new Guardian style columnist Stephen Libby – might be worth a read).
Burnett tells me a story: when she was deputy manager of an Oxfam shop in the early 90s, lads from the local school would shove each other over the threshold, such was the teenage shame of setting foot in a charity shop.
“Now I see younger and younger generations 100% embracing secondhand clothing. It’s fantastic for charity shops and it’s great for the planet,” she says.

Little Bird | ★★★★☆
Few dramas will enrage you as much as Little Bird. Not because it’s in any way hokey or problematic. On the contrary. Based on the real story of the Sixties Scoop – a period in Canada from the mid-1950s to the 1980s, when an estimated 20,000 First Nations children were forcibly removed from their families and adopted by non-Indigenous families – this heartbreaking tale is restrained and carefully measured. Melodrama is swerved, letting the injustice at this story’s core slowly metastasise. Little Bird is an impressive and heartfelt work, tender and moving. It cleaned up at the Canadian Screen Awards. For it to be ignored globally would be a crime. Patrick Smith
Music
   Lambchop: Punching the Clown | ★★★★☆
 Thirty-two years on from their debut album, Lambchop find themselves in a curious position. Their sole continuous member Kurt Wagner has displayed an admirable disinclination to rest on his laurels. Their last album, 2022’s The Bible, threw up everything from house music to glitchy rhythms to ambient drift to accompany Wagner’s pained ruminations on mortality and faith. Punching the Clown, pares back their sound to bare essentials: acoustic guitar and banjo and the very occasional deployment of bass or piano, the faintest smear of electronics on Weakened. Wagner’s voice appears stripped of Auto-Tune, distortion, even reverb: he sounds as if he’s singing directly in front of you. Alexis Petridis
Film
Over/Under | ★★★★☆
 Practically any woman who had a best female friend in early adolescence will be able to relate to this fragile, thoughtful drama about two American children, Violet (Emajean Bullock) and Stella (Anastasia Veronica Lee), living through the ages of nine to 13. As the film starts, the two are nine-year-old besties, spending their summers together in New England where they go to camp. But when both girls go home at the end of the summer, Violet to Los Angeles and Stella to San Diego, life is not so dreamy and blissful. Violet is bullied at school. Plus, it looks like her parents’ marriage is on the rocks. Stella too has worries, especially around the survival of her mother (Madeline Wise) who copes throughout with breast cancer, while her father (Adam David Thompson) is contending with an off-screen mother with dementia. Leslie Felperin
Game
Agent 64: Spies Never Die (PC) | ★★★☆☆
 In lieu of any high-budget flash, Agent 64’s big special effect is nostalgia. From the title onwards, this retro shooter is one long homage to nineties James Bond shoot-em-up GoldenEye, and to its un-Bonded successor, 2000’s Perfect Dark. Enemies have pinched facial features – a result of taking photographs of real people’s faces and wrapping them around diamond-shaped heads – and roll acrobatically from behind cover to take their next potshot, just as they used to. And yes, there’s a Big Head mode that swells those diamonds into enormous target-practice balloons. The fantasy on offer here isn’t really being James Bond. It’s being young again, with one illicitly acquired copy of GoldenEye to last you the summer and all the time in the world to pick the cartridge clean. For all its rough edges, that’s a mission Agent 64 pulls off with aplomb. Alex Spencer.

James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz were novice gardeners when they made the move from inner-city Chicago out to the Illinois suburbs. They knew one thing, though: that they didn’t simply want their front garden to be a piece of turf – so they set about transforming it through rewilding.
What was once a boring lawn is now a thriving ecosystem that attracts and supports birds, butterflies, bees, rabbits, bats, foxes and more, while their efforts have been recognised by the National Wildlife Federation, who designated the space a Certified Wildlife Habitat. “It’s really a stunning environment,” says McGuire. “It brings us a lot of peace and tranquility in a very troubled world.”

items.body:
It was a slower quarter for “high-heat footwear product”, said JD Sports. It didn’t mean it was struggling to shift sandals during a heatwave. Rather, it was referring coyly to the big global trainer brands’ failure to come up with hot new designs. When Nike and Adidas, reckoned by City analysts to account for slightly more than half JD’s sales, are on tepid form, the self-styled “king of trainers” retailer usually is as well.
The low-heat grumble will be familiar to JD’s shareholders. So, too, the one about “incremental cost of living pressures”, especially in the US. And the phrase “a promotional market” has appeared so often in the company’s updates in the past couple of years that it would be easier to tell us when discounting isn’t dominant.
The result was another warning on profits and a 14% slump in the share price. JD now thinks it’ll make between £700m and £800m at an underlying pre-tax level this financial year. The difference from the previous estimate of £750m-£850m isn’t huge, but they all count. This was the third warning since early 2024. The particular disappointment this time is that it was a men’s football World Cup year, which ought to have been good for generating a general sporty buzz for a global business.
The market clearly is genuinely weak. Nike’s share price is down a third this year even after a miserable performance in the last two. Or look at Adidas’s own recent warning that its big marketing bet on the World Cup didn’t pay off. Or at the sluggish spending among US consumers in response to higher energy prices: Walmart, the largest US retailer, this week reported its slowest sales growth in six years.
Even so, the deeper worry at JD is that the whole “athleisure” trend isn’t coming back – or, if it does, at nothing like the level of the old days. The Covid pandemic created a mini-boom for joggers and trainers but since then the direction has only been one way. Did Nike and Adidas push prices too far? Have they been outflanked by the likes of Hoka and On? Or have consumer tastes just changed? Probably all of the above to an extent – and none is good news for JD.
The cashflow forecast, for £460m-£520m, didn’t change, which is evidence to support JD’s boasts about sharpening internal controls after its previous boom years of successful global expansion in the 2010s. All the same, waiting for an upturn, counting the cashflow and buying back a few shares makes for an uninspiring life.
Disagreements about strategy reportedly led to the exit of the chair, Andrew Higginson, last month, and it is easy to see why there would be tension. The share price is back at 2019 levels. If this were a conventionally owned public company, as opposed to one with a 55% shareholder in the form of the Pentland Group, the chief executive Régis Schultz might be under more pressure to generate some trading heat via self-help. Non-Pentland shareholders are surely frustrated.
